items.title: Investigating a remote IT worker scam: A field guide for DFIR teams
items.summary: By Steve Gemperle Key takeaways The remote IT worker scam starts with hiring, so investigators need HR, payroll, and vendor records alongside endpoint and log data. Shipping a laptop to a facilitator’s address makes a remote worker appear to be in the U.S. Comparing the shipping address, IP addresses, VPN exits, and MFA enrollment location against the claimed residence can expose it. No single red flag proves fraud. Several indicators that point to the same address, device, or payment destination are a stronger signal. Preserve evidence before disabling access, then work out whether the worker only collected wages or also exfiltrated data. The remote IT worker scam starts with a job application. Like many forms of digital fraud , it relies on trust: the organization believes it’s hiring a real person and hands over access accordingly. A worker using a false identity may pass interviews, receive a company laptop, and gain legitimate access to the organization’s systems. Behind that apparently routine onboarding process may be U.S.-based facilitators, laptop farms, remote access tools, and arrangements that divert wages to other parties. In some cases, the activity extends to data theft or extortion. That means investigators have two questions to answer: how the fraud was carried out, and what the worker did once inside. The evidence is split across hiring and identity records, device activity, login locations, payment records, repository activity, and communications. This guide covers how the scam works, the red flags to watch for, what to collect, and a step-by-step investigation workflow. If you’re already gathering evidence from other teams, skip to the sample evidence request list . How the remote IT worker scam works These scams typically move through a series of stages, from building a false identity to drawing wages and, in some cases, taking data. Each stage touches a different part of the organization, which is why the investigation has to span HR, IT, security, and finance. Identity preparation: The actor uses a stolen, synthetic, borrowed, or facilitator-supported identity. Resume content, portfolio sites, job board profiles, social media, payment accounts, and identification documents are created or altered to support the cover story. Hiring channel entry: The actor applies through direct hiring, staffing vendors, freelance platforms, or contractor pipelines. The technical skill may be real, which helps the candidate appear credible. Interview support: A domestic facilitator, proxy, AI tool, or scripted response process helps the actor pass video interviews. Some signs to watch include mismatched identity details, unusual delays in responses, inconsistent audio/video behavior, or answers that feel scripted. Device placement: Once the worker is hired, the company ships a laptop to an address controlled by a domestic facilitator. The facilitator keeps the device and connects it to a domestic location or reships it. This creates the appearance that the worker is operating from inside the U.S. Remote operation: The actual worker connects through remote desktop software, VPNs, VPS infrastructure, residential proxies, or other tunneling methods to use the company-issued device. Revenue and access abuse: The wages are routed through bank accounts, payment processors, cryptocurrency, or third parties. In higher-risk cases, the worker may copy source code, harvest credentials, access cloud storage, or extort the company after discovery. Common red flags No single indicator proves fraud, and some may have reasonable explanations. The signs below are most useful when several appear together or point back to the same address, device, or payment destination. Multiple workers or applicants sharing the same address, phone number, emergency contact, profile language, resume structure, device shipping location, or payment destination. Identity documents with inconsistent formatting, mismatched metadata, low-quality edits, altered headshots, or details that do not align with payroll, tax, HR, or background check records. Logins from countries, VPN providers, data centers, or residential proxy networks that do not match the worker’s claimed location. Company laptop showing signs of unattended remote control, remote desktop tools , remote administration utilities, unauthorized VPN clients, tunneling software, or persistent access agents. Unusual work patterns, such as activity during local sleeping hours, rapid context switching between accounts, or repeated short sessions from different IP addresses. Use of personal cloud storage, private code repositories, mass data transfer, compressed archives, or file movement outside approved channels. Requests to avoid video calls, change payment methods, route compensation to a third party, or ship devices to addresses that do not match verified residence details. Digital forensics collection priorities The evidence in these cases is spread across teams that each hold part of the picture. The table below sets out the main sources, what to collect from each, and why it matters. Evidence source What to collect Why it matters Endpoint Full disk image or targeted collection, installed programs, prefetch, event logs, browser artifacts, remote access configuration, scheduled tasks, persistence locations, USB history, clipboard and recent file artifacts where available. Shows whether the company device was remotely controlled, used by multiple operators, or configured to bypass policy. Identity and access logs SSO logs, MFA registrations, IP addresses, device IDs, user-agent strings, impossible travel alerts, session tokens, conditional access events, failed logins, and authentication method changes. Establishes the real access pattern and whether the account was used from inconsistent locations or devices. Network telemetry VPN logs, firewall logs, DNS, proxy logs, EDR network connections, RDP/remote tool traffic, data center IPs, residential proxy indicators, and unusual outbound connections. Helps identify remote control infrastructure and tunneling behavior. Cloud and SaaS Email, chat, file sharing, source code platform events, repository cloning, API token creation, OAuth grants, file downloads, sharing events, and personal account connections. Determines whether data was copied, staged, shared, or exfiltrated. HR and payroll Application records, interview recordings if retained, identity documents, address history, tax records, payment routing, emergency contact data, vendor records, and device shipment details. Connects technical evidence to fraud indicators and facilitator infrastructure. For a more detailed list organized by team, see the sample evidence request list below. Practical investigation workflow The order of operations matters. Disabling access or confronting the worker too early can alert them before evidence is preserved. The steps below put preservation first. Stabilize quietly: Preserve logs and avoid alerting the suspected worker until counsel, HR, security, and leadership agree on the response plan. It is important to be able to covertly collect from the endpoint in question. Scope the identity: Build a timeline from application through onboarding, device shipment, first login, tool installation, repository access, payroll changes, and any suspicious data movement. Correlate locations: Compare claimed residence, device shipping address, payroll address, IP geolocation, VPN exits, MFA enrollment location, and remote desktop source locations. Analyze the endpoint: Look for remote administration tools, secondary users, unusual startup entries, unauthorized browser profiles, copied credentials, cloud sync clients, and artifacts showing hands-on-keyboard activity inconsistent with the claimed user. Review code and data access: Identify repositories cloned, branches accessed, secrets viewed, archives created, large downloads, remote access to build or deployment systems, and connections to personal cloud or developer accounts. Map facilitators: Search for shared addresses, payment accounts, phone numbers, shipping labels, vendor contacts, front company websites, and repeated resume or portfolio patterns across other employees or applicants. Assess impact: Determine whether the worker only received wages under false pretenses or also accessed, copied, altered, or exfiltrated sensitive data. Coordinate response: Preserve evidence, disable access in a controlled sequence, recover company equipment where feasible, rotate exposed credentials, revoke tokens, notify legal and compliance teams, and prepare law enforcement reporting. Key forensic questions to answer These questions help keep the investigation focused on what the organization needs to determine, from who controlled the account to which legal obligations apply. Who actually controlled the account, and from where? Was the company-issued device physically located where the worker claimed to be? Were unauthorized remote access tools installed or used? Did the worker copy source code, secrets, customer data, export-controlled material, financial data, or credentials? Were personal cloud accounts, private repositories, cryptocurrency wallets, or third-party payment accounts involved? Are there other applicants, contractors, or employees with overlapping indicators? Did any vendor or staffing agency fail to validate identity or device custody? What legal, sanctions, notification, contractual, and law enforcement obligations are triggered? Containment and remediation When the evidence supports acting, containment should happen in a planned sequence rather than all at once. The goal is to remove the worker’s access completely without destroying records the investigation still needs. Disable account access only after critical logs are preserved and the response team is ready. Revoke active sessions, refresh tokens, OAuth grants, SSH keys, API keys, personal access tokens, and developer credentials. Rotate secrets that were accessible to the worker, including repository secrets, cloud keys, service account credentials, build pipeline tokens, and database credentials. Block unauthorized remote access tools and review endpoint policy exceptions. Quarantine or collect affected devices, then validate whether the device was physically hosted by a facilitator. Search for related indicators across other employees, applicants, contractors, and vendors. Review vendor agreements, background check procedures, device shipping controls, and sanctions screening processes. Prevention tips for investigators and security teams Many of the gaps these schemes exploit sit between teams. The controls below focus on verifying identity, device custody, and access, and on getting HR, IT, security, payroll, and vendor data in front of the same people. Require strong identity proofing for remote workers before access is granted and repeat verification during employment when risk indicators appear. Verify that the person interviewed is the person onboarded, paid, and using the device. Ship devices only to verified addresses and require secure device enrollment before production access. Use conditional access policies that restrict logins by device compliance, geography, impossible travel, and unmanaged devices. Maintain an approved remote access software list and alert on unauthorized tools. Monitor developer environments for mass cloning, personal repository use, unusual compression, secret access, and large downloads. Correlate HR, IT, security, payroll, and vendor data rather than leaving each team to review its own silo. Create a playbook specifically for remote IT worker fraud investigations so the organization does not improvise during an active case. Sample evidence request list Use this list as a practical starting point when issuing preservation notices, internal evidence requests, or third-party collection requests. Tailor the scope to the suspected worker, relevant dates, legal hold requirements, and the systems actually used by the organization. 1. Human resources and recruiting Candidate application package, resume versions, cover letters, portfolio links, job board submissions, and recruiter notes. Interview schedules, interviewer feedback, video interview recordings (if retained), chat transcripts, assessment results, and coding test submissions. Identity-verification records, background check reports, work-authorization documents, tax forms, address records, and any exceptions or manual overrides. Onboarding records, offer letters, employment agreements, contractor agreements, confidentiality agreements, and security policy acknowledgments. Emergency contact information, personal phone numbers, personal email addresses, mailing addresses, and any changes made after onboarding. Records showing whether the same address, phone number, reference, recruiter, staffing vendor, or emergency contact appears across other candidates or workers. 2. IT asset management and endpoint team Device assignment records, serial numbers, hostnames, asset tags, device enrollment dates, assigned users, and custody history. Shipping records, tracking numbers, delivery confirmation, recipient names, delivery addresses, return labels, and any reshipment information. Endpoint management records, compliance state, installed software inventory, local user accounts, administrative group membership, firewall settings, and configuration profiles. EDR telemetry, process execution, network connections, file creation events, persistence artifacts, remote access tool detections, and suspicious command-line activity. Operating system event logs, authentication logs, remote desktop logs, prefetch artifacts, browser artifacts, cloud sync artifacts, USB history, and recent file activity. Records of help desk tickets, password reset requests, MFA reset requests, device troubleshooting, remote support sessions, and unusual access requests. 3. Identity, security operations, and network teams SSO logs, MFA enrollment history, conditional access events, failed and successful login records, session duration, user-agent strings, device identifiers, and authentication method changes. VPN logs, proxy logs, DNS logs, firewall logs, secure web gateway records, ZTNA records, and remote access gateway logs. Alerts related to impossible travel, anonymous proxy usage, data center IP addresses, residential proxy activity, suspicious token use, or unmanaged device access. Cloud identity records, OAuth consent grants, personal access tokens, API keys, SSH keys, service account use, privilege changes, and group membership changes. Security alerts, incident tickets, analyst notes, case timelines, prior investigations, and any related indicators tied to other employees, contractors, or applicants. 4. Cloud, email, collaboration, and source code platforms Email mailbox exports or targeted searches for onboarding, payroll, vendor, personal email, shipping, credential, and file sharing terms. Chat messages, channel membership, direct messages, file transfers, meeting participation, and communications with external accounts. Cloud storage audit logs, file downloads, sharing events, external shares, deleted files, synchronization activity, and access from personal or unmanaged devices. Source code repository logs, repository cloning, branch access, pull requests, commits, fork activity, deployment access, package registry activity, and private remote configurations. Secret management access logs, build pipeline logs, artifact downloads, container registry activity, and infrastructure-as-code repository access. 5. Payroll, finance, and procurement Payroll setup records, bank account details, payment change history, direct deposit forms, tax forms, payment processors, and third-party payment instructions. Invoices, vendor payment records, contractor statements of work, purchase orders, timekeeping records, expense reports, and reimbursement requests. Records showing payment routing to accounts that do not match the worker’s claimed identity, address, tax information, or employment arrangement. Any cryptocurrency-related payment requests, unusual payment timing, split payments, or requests to route funds through another individual or entity. Vendor master data, staffing agency records, recruiter payment information, and any shared financial indicators across multiple workers or candidates. 6. Staffing vendors, recruiters, and third parties Candidate sourcing records, recruiter communications, screening notes, background check documents, identity-verification records, and interview logistics. Copies of contracts, statements of work, work orders, invoices, and vendor compliance attestations. Device shipping instructions, mailing addresses, contact names, phone numbers, alternate email addresses, and any request to route hardware through another party. Records identifying whether the same recruiter, account manager, address, payment destination, or phone number appears across multiple candidates. Vendor security reviews, due diligence records, contractual identity proofing requirements, and any notice of prior suspicious activity involving the same vendor. 7. Legal, compliance, and case management Legal hold notices, preservation instructions, investigation scope memos, privilege protocols, and chain-of-custody documentation. Applicable contracts, nondisclosure agreements, acceptable use policies, sanctions screening records, data classification guidance, and notification requirements. Prior incident reports, related hotline complaints, insider risk referrals, vendor risk findings, and law enforcement correspondence if already initiated. Decision logs showing when access was preserved, restricted, disabled, or restored, and who approved each action. Final evidence index, custodian list, systems searched, search terms used, collection dates, gaps, and unresolved follow-up items. Bringing it all together A suspected remote IT worker scam rarely comes into focus from a single log entry or an unusual interview. The picture becomes clearer when investigators bring the hiring records, device activity, access logs, and payment trail together and test what they find against reasonable explanations. Preserve the evidence, document what is known and what remains uncertain, and keep HR, legal, and security working from the same facts. That approach gives the organization a sound basis for protecting its people and data, responding fairly, and closing the gaps that allowed the scam to take hold. About the author Steve Gemperle is the Manger of Technical Marketing and Forensics at Magnet Forensics. Prior to joining Magnet, Steve was a Senior Special Agent with the United States Secret Service who specialized in cyber-crime until retiring in 2021. For the last decade of his career with the Secret Service he focused on computer crimes and served as Lab Director for the US Secret Service Southwest Regional Computer Forensic Lab. Steve has completed over 1900 forensic exams and 150 network intrusion investigations while working for the Secret Service, and has been recognized as one of the US Secret Service’s top network intrusion investigators.

items.title: Report: Online Scams Nearly Doubled in 2026
items.summary: A new report from Akamai has found that online scams surpassed traditional phishing attacks for the first time in 2026, nearly doubling from about 3.2 million to approximately 6.4 million year-over-year. The researchers say this signals a “shift toward higher-return fraud tactics focused on direct financial and consumer deception.”

That's a lie that they excuse by saying it'll come true soon: https://pluralistic.net/2024/12/04/its-not-a-lie/#its-a-premature-truth Elon Musk is the world's most enthusiastic teller of these lies. That's not surprising: any kind of radical promise about the automotive sector has a 90% chance of being this kind of bullshit. Musk can barely mention the subject of transportation without lying his face off: from "full self-driving" to "hyperloops" to "tunnels" to "flying cars," Musk is a fountain of extremely untrue "premature truths": https://karlbode.com/musks-fake-flying-car-and-ceo-said-a-thing-journalism/ But Musk has plenty of competition when it comes to lies about futuristic cars. Long before Musk switched on his first bullshit factory, Uber was spending billions to spray the world with lies about cars. Uber has always lied about everything, from driver pay to the company's finances. Now, lying about driver pay is relatively low-risk for a company like Uber. After all, the company created the app-based worker misclassification playbook, designed to make vulnerable and precarious workers even more vulnerable and precarious. The lies Uber tells about its workforce only have to survive contact with credulous municipal governments so that they keep up a supply of get-out-of-jail-free cards for Uber's many labor, licensing and consumer rights violations. But lying about your finances is another matter altogether. When Uber lies about its finances, it is lying to rich people, and (unlike workers), rich people have many ways to punish people who lie to them. Despite this, Uber spent more than a decade lying flagrantly and lavishly about its balance sheet. The most shameless financial lie Uber told is that it was profitable due to the increased valuation of the many ride-hailing companies around the world that Uber owns large shares in. How did Uber come to own large shares in these companies? It happened after Uber's competing ride-hailing companies in countries around the world failed. Uber's subsidiaries lost billions of dollars, and eventually Uber sold them to its (also money-losing) domestic rivals in all-stock deals that saw Uber acquiring vast amounts of worthless, illiquid shares in the world's failing ride-hailing companies. Then, for years , Uber would announce that its stake in these companies had appreciated in value. These revaluations were purely vibes-based. Uber's former rivals were privately held, and while small volumes of shares traded hands in private deals, Uber's pronouncements that, say, the Chinese company Didi was now worth vastly more than it had been worth a few months before was sheer fantasy dressed up as profits: https://pluralistic.net/2022/02/11/bezzlers-gonna-bezzle/#gryft Uber did this over and over (and over and over), relentlessly dogged by Hubert Horan, an aviation analyst who became the world's foremost close-reader of Uber's financial statements: https://pluralistic.net/2023/08/09/accounting-gimmicks/#unter Despite these lies, Uber eventually found a way for its early investors to cash out, through a very successful IPO that saw the House of Saud made whole (and then some) on the $31b they plowed into the business so that it could lose $0.41 on every dollar it brought in for the preceding 13 years. The most remarkable thing about Uber's IPO was the company's S1, the prospectus that tells normie investors how the company will eventually find its way to profit. That's where you'll find Uber's claim that its "total addressable market" is every journey made by taxi, private car, train and bus, for everyone in the world : https://stratechery.com/2019/uber-questions/ Despite the wild implausibility of this ambition, the company did achieve actual profitability after its IPO. It got there through the simple expedient of paying drivers less and charging riders more. The company spies on its drivers to calculate the lowest wage they'll accept, based on their inferred economic desperation, a process that Veena Dubal calls "algorithmic wage discrimination": https://pluralistic.net/2023/04/12/algorithmic-wage-discrimination/#fishers-of-men They also use surveillance data about riders to calculate the highest price you'll pay for a journey. Investors call this "personalized pricing," while everyone else calls it "surveillance pricing." It's a way for Uber to reach into your bank account and reduce the value of your dollars, by charging you more than the next person would pay for the same service: https://pluralistic.net/2025/06/24/price-discrimination/ This is something AI turns out to be extremely good at. Businesses can program chatbots to automatically segment their customers and employees based on surveillance data and then perform a series of automated experiments to find the highest prices and lowest wages they'll accept: https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/30/pay-for-privacy/#ab2654 When it comes to wage theft and price gouging, Uber leads the pack. They've really demonstrated just how much consumer and labor surplus can be diverted to capital with the aid of AI. Of course, it helps that they're willing to lie like crazy. Uber routinely claims that it pays its drivers hourly rates that are far in excess of minimum wage, but it helpfully omits that drivers only get paid while they have a passenger in the car, and that the company punishes drivers who turn down too many unprofitable jobs. Drivers only get paid for a fraction of the time they spend working for Uber, and on top of that, they have to pay for fuel, insurance, depreciation, loan interest, and the cost of getting vomit out of their back seats. Add it all up and Uber drivers make peanuts. In Toronto, Uber pay nets out to something like $2.50/hour: https://pluralistic.net/2024/02/29/geometry-hates-uber/#toronto-the-gullible $2.50/hour isn't a living wage anywhere in Canada, but it's especially terrible in Toronto, one of the world's most expensive cities. Uber can only be profitable for so long as drivers continue to subsidize its business, and so long as riders are willing to pay more than they ever did under the traditional taxi system (much of which was seen off by Uber's Saudi-subsidized decade of predatory pricing, which also induced a lost decade in global transit investment). Inflation (supercharged by AI pricing) has hit all workers, but it's been especially hard on Uber drivers, who didn't have any financial cushion to start with. Eventually, drivers were bound to turn their backs on Uber. "Eventually" is now, according to Uber's Q3 earnings call, where CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told investors that "driver supply [was] not keeping pace with strong consumer demand in several international markets": https://s23.q4cdn.com/407969754/files/doc_earnings/2026/q3/earnings-result/Uber-Q3-26-Earnings-Press-Release.pdf As The Gig Economy Project writes, the driver shortage is especially sharp in India and Brazil, two gigantic countries where (according to Uber CFO Balaji Krishnamurthy), there is too much consumer "price sensitivity": https://thegigeconomyproject.substack.com/p/has-uber-finally-pushed-its-workers Uber's also having trouble getting drivers to accept the rock-bottom wages they're offering for food delivery. Despite this, Krishnamurthy assured investors that the company's measures to "improve driver availability" wouldn't affect their bottom line. Instead, Krishnamurthy promised to raise prices on riders elsewhere, something he called "re-balancing incentives": That is part of the art that we’ve got and then there is a lot of algorithmic science that goes into, if you have a dollar, what is the maximum predicted return for that dollar and should I invest that dollar in a driver in Brazil or should I invest that dollar in a rider in India, for example. The algorithm can structurally make these choices based on training on billions of trips and allocate these investments in the way that humans just can’t. The Gig Economy Project goes on to say that "robotaxis will fundamentally alter the unit economics of taxis, but we are still some time away from the point where robotaxis are price competitive with human-driven vehicles." Boy is this an understatement . Remember, Uber is already paying drivers sub-minimum, sub-starvation wages, which drivers must spend to cover all the capital, depreciation, maintenance and insurance costs, along with (skyrocketing) fuel costs. I can't think of any way in which replacing starvation-wage drivers who provide their own cars with $200k robotaxis that the company must operate, maintain and insure will work out better for the company than the current situation. This is as good as it gets for Uber, in other words. Being able to tap an army of desperate workers who supply 99% of Uber's business's capital and variable costs out of their own pockets is vastly superior to operating a fleet of expensive robots that Uber has to purchase and service. Profitable "driverless" cars have been around the corner for more than 15 years now. Waymo claims to have delivered this through the brute force expedient of using the most expensive sensors and vast amounts of incredibly expensive cloud computing, but their balance sheet remains stubbornly opaque. We don't know how often a "driverless" Waymo is just a remote control car, being piloted by a low-wage worker in an overseas call center (there's a reason Indian technologists joke that AI stands for "Absent Indians"): https://pluralistic.net/2024/01/29/pay-no-attention/#to-the-little-man-behind-the-curtain We also don't know how often a Waymo is being overseen by a high -waged engineer. What we do know is that that when GM was forced to reveal this number, it turned out that they'd replaced a single, low-waged cab driver with 1.5 engineers, each of whom earned an order of magnitude more than the cabbie they'd displaced: https://garymarcus.substack.com/p/could-cruise-be-the-theranos-of-ai Uber's claims that they were profitable (based on accounting gimmicks) were lies, but they were also premature truths: the company did become profitable (though price-gouging and wage-theft). But there's a limit to how low you can push your workforce's wages, and even if the AI crash delivers a fresh cohort of desperate workers who subsidize Uber's operations for a few more years, they, too, will eventually find that they can't live on $2.50/hour. When that day comes, robo-taxis won't save the business model. Robots may cost less per hour than Uber drivers (though not by much), but owning a robot is always going to be more expensive than getting drivers to supply free cars to Uber. If Uber can't sustain profitability with that massive subsidy, it is going to hit a wall, and it won't be pretty. Profitable "driverless" cars have been around the corner for more than 15 years now. Waymo claims to have delivered this through the brute force expedient of using the most expensive sensors and vast amounts of incredibly expensive cloud computing, but their balance sheet remains stubbornly opaque. We don't know how often a "driverless" Waymo is just a remote control car, being piloted by a low-wage worker in an overseas call center (there's a reason Indian technologists joke that AI stands for "Absent Indians"):

https://pluralistic.net/2024/01/29/pay-no-attention/#to-the-little-man-behind-the-curtain

We also don't know how often a Waymo is being overseen by a high-waged engineer. What we do know is that that when GM was forced to reveal this number, it turned out that they'd replaced a single, low-waged cab driver with 1.5 engineers, each of whom earned an order of magnitude more than the cabbie they'd displaced:

https://garymarcus.substack.com/p/could-cruise-be-the-theranos-of-ai

Uber's claims that they were profitable (based on accounting gimmicks) were lies, but they were also premature truths: the company did become profitable (though price-gouging and wage-theft). But there's a limit to how low you can push your workforce's wages, and even if the AI crash delivers a fresh cohort of desperate workers who subsidize Uber's operations for a few more years, they, too, will eventually find that they can't live on $2.50/hour.

When that day comes, robo-taxis won't save the business model. Robots may cost less per hour than Uber drivers (though not by much), but owning a robot is always going to be more expensive than getting drivers to supply free cars to Uber. If Uber can't sustain profitability with that massive subsidy, it is going to hit a wall, and it won't be pretty.

items.title: Security Agencies Worldwide Found to Use Ad-Based Surveillance System
items.summary: An investigation by Bloomberg into Penlink’s ad-based surveillance system Webloc builds off Citizen Lab research, identifying additional customers of the tracking technology. The findings that Webloc has been acquired by security agencies in a number of countries aligns with potential customers we identified in our April report. Senior researcher Wolfie Christl notes that Webloc “is a powerful mass surveillance tool that’s trickling down from military and intelligence agencies to federal law enforcement and then to state and local police.” Our report used open source research, freedom of information requests, and server infrastructure mapping to identify Webloc customers in the US, El Salvador, and Hungary. Since then, the Austrian Ministry of the Interior has also been confirmed as a customer. The Bloomberg investigation identified customers in additional countries including the UK, Netherlands, Germany, Mexico, Singapore, Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Israel. The lawfulness of using these systems in Europe and the UK is highly controversial . While intrusive and disproportionate ad-based mass surveillance is problematic everywhere, its use in authoritarian countries identified by reporting is particularly dangerous. Read Bloomberg’s investigation Read our “Uncovering Webloc” report

items.title: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618): How Imperva Protects Customers
items.summary: A critical vulnerability was disclosed today in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server, one of the most widely deployed web servers in the world. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618 , the flaw could allow a remote attacker to run code on an affected server without authenticating. Here is what we know, and how Imperva customers are protected. What is the vulnerability? CVE-2026-119618 affects mod_http2, the Apache module that implements the HTTP/2 protocol. It has been rated 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS severity scale. An attacker who can reach a vulnerable server over HTTP/2 can potentially take control of the server process, with no credentials required. The flaw affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, as well as standalone builds of the mod_h2 module. Only servers that have HTTP/2 enabled are exposed. The Apache project has released version 2.4.71, which fixes the issue, and operating system vendors are publishing patched packages on their own schedules. Public reports differ on whether a working exploit exists. We recommend treating this vulnerability as a serious risk and acting accordingly. Are Imperva products affected? Imperva Cloud WAF and Imperva WAF Gateway are not affected by this vulnerability. How Imperva Cloud WAF protects customers Cloud WAF sites are onboarded without HTTP/2 support by default, so customers who have not changed this setting are protected out of the box. The attack traffic never reaches their origin server. Customers who have enabled HTTP/2 can remain protected by choosing only the “HTTP/2 client to Imperva” option. With this option, HTTP/2 is handled at Imperva and the attack traffic doesn’t reach the origin. How Imperva WAF Gateway protects customers When deployed in reverse proxy mode with HTTP/2 support disabled, WAF Gateway drops HTTP/2 traffic, blocking this attack. Customers who have enabled HTTP/2 can mitigate this risk by disabling HTTP/2 support in their WAF Gateway Web Service configuration. This prevents HTTP/2 attack traffic from reaching their origin servers. For deployments running in bridge mode, where HTTP/2 traffic is passed through to the origin, customers should take additional steps to protect their Apache servers. How Imperva for Google Cloud, Imperva for AWS, and Elastic WAF protect customers Imperva for Google Cloud Customers using HTTP/2 between the Google Cloud Global Load Balancer and their backend servers should change their Backend Service Protocol to HTTPS (HTTP/1.1 over TLS). This mitigation is configured directly in Google Cloud, rather than through the Imperva console. Imperva for AWS Customers whose traffic passes through Amazon CloudFront are already protected against this attack path, as CloudFront communicates with origin servers using HTTP/1.1, preventing HTTP/2 attack traffic from reaching the origin. Elastic WAF Customers using HTTP/2 between their Ingress Controller and backend services should reconfigure this connection to use HTTPS over HTTP/1.1 instead. We recommend these configuration changes as an immediate mitigation for affected deployments. Imperva is investigating additional mitigation capabilities and will provide updates as they become available. What should you do now? Regardless of how you deploy Imperva, we recommend identifying any Apache HTTP Server instances in your environment that have HTTP/2 enabled and applying the vendor fix as soon as it is available for your platform. Review your HTTP/2 settings in your Imperva configuration to confirm which of the protections above applies to you. Our teams continue to investigate additional mitigation options for customers who need to maintain HTTP/2 support and will provide updates as they become available. Need help? For details about your specific configuration, or help reviewing and changing your HTTP/2 settings, please contact Imperva Support. We will continue to update this post as our investigation progresses.

A critical vulnerability was disclosed today in the HTTP/2 module of Apache HTTP Server, one of the most widely deployed web servers in the world. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618, the flaw could allow a remote attacker to run code on an affected server without authenticating. Here is what we know, and how Imperva customers are protected. 

What is the vulnerability? 

CVE-2026-119618 affects mod_http2, the Apache module that implements the HTTP/2 protocol. It has been rated 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS severity scale. An attacker who can reach a vulnerable server over HTTP/2 can potentially take control of the server process, with no credentials required. 

The flaw affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, as well as standalone builds of the mod_h2 module. Only servers that have HTTP/2 enabled are exposed. The Apache project has released version 2.4.71, which fixes the issue, and operating system vendors are publishing patched packages on their own schedules. 

Public reports differ on whether a working exploit exists. We recommend treating this vulnerability as a serious risk and acting accordingly. 

Are Imperva products affected? 

Imperva Cloud WAF and Imperva WAF Gateway are not affected by this vulnerability. 

How Imperva Cloud WAF protects customers 

Cloud WAF sites are onboarded without HTTP/2 support by default, so customers who have not changed this setting are protected out of the box. The attack traffic never reaches their origin server. 

Customers who have enabled HTTP/2 can remain protected by choosing only the “HTTP/2 client to Imperva” option. With this option, HTTP/2 is handled at Imperva and the attack traffic doesn’t reach the origin. 

How Imperva WAF Gateway protects customers 

When deployed in reverse proxy mode with HTTP/2 support disabled, WAF Gateway drops HTTP/2 traffic, blocking this attack. Customers who have enabled HTTP/2 can mitigate this risk by disabling HTTP/2 support in their WAF Gateway Web Service configuration. This prevents HTTP/2 attack traffic from reaching their origin servers. For deployments running in bridge mode, where HTTP/2 traffic is passed through to the origin, customers should take additional steps to protect their Apache servers.  

How Imperva for Google Cloud, Imperva for AWS, and Elastic WAF protect customers Imperva for Google Cloud

Customers using HTTP/2 between the Google Cloud Global Load Balancer and their backend servers should change their Backend Service Protocol to HTTPS (HTTP/1.1 over TLS). This mitigation is configured directly in Google Cloud, rather than through the Imperva console.

Imperva for AWS

Customers whose traffic passes through Amazon CloudFront are already protected against this attack path, as CloudFront communicates with origin servers using HTTP/1.1, preventing HTTP/2 attack traffic from reaching the origin.

Elastic WAF

Customers using HTTP/2 between their Ingress Controller and backend services should reconfigure this connection to use HTTPS over HTTP/1.1 instead.

We recommend these configuration changes as an immediate mitigation for affected deployments. Imperva is investigating additional mitigation capabilities and will provide updates as they become available.

What should you do now? 

Regardless of how you deploy Imperva, we recommend identifying any Apache HTTP Server instances in your environment that have HTTP/2 enabled and applying the vendor fix as soon as it is available for your platform. Review your HTTP/2 settings in your Imperva configuration to confirm which of the protections above applies to you.  

Our teams continue to investigate additional mitigation options for customers who need to maintain HTTP/2 support and will provide updates as they become available. 

Need help? 

For details about your specific configuration, or help reviewing and changing your HTTP/2 settings, please contact Imperva Support. We will continue to update this post as our investigation progresses.

items.title: How Fidelis Security Strengthens Azure Zero Trust Beyond Identity and Access
items.summary: Key Takeaways Azure Zero Trust goes beyond authentication. Compromised identities and workloads can misuse legitimate access, making continuous monitoring essential. Azure Zero Trust requires monitoring beyond network segmentation. Fidelis helps detect suspicious activity within permitted network connections. Fidelis Active Directory Intercept helps detect Kerberos abuse, AD reconnaissance, and lateral movement, strengthening protection across hybrid environments. Fidelis supports the assume-breach approach with deep network inspection, deception, workload risk assessment, and XDR. Fidelis strengthens Zero Trust investigations by helping SOC teams connect evidence, assess the impact of a compromise, and coordinate response. An employee signs in through Microsoft Entra ID, completes their authentication, and accesses an app they are authorized to use. Now imagine an attacker has gained access to the employee’s authenticated session or device. The access may still satisfy the organization’s policies, but the person or process using it may no longer be trustworthy. The attacker can potentially access resources available to the employee, explore connected systems, and attempt to steal sensitive information. Microsoft Azure provides strong identity and access controls, but successful authentication does not guarantee legitimate activity. An effective Azure Zero Trust implementation must also detect and investigate threats involving compromised credentials, authenticated sessions, and permitted connections. Microsoft’s 2026 Digital Defense Report [1] found that 52.2% of intrusions involving valid accounts included follow-on credential theft. It also found that 63% of observed intrusions involved data theft. At Fidelis , we help organizations put the assume-breach principle into practice. Our solutions complement Microsoft’s controls by helping security teams identify suspicious behavior, investigate threats within permitted access paths, and respond across Azure and hybrid environments. Let’s look at how these capabilities support the security requirements of an Azure Zero Trust architecture. What Security Controls are Included in Azure Zero Trust? Microsoft’s Zero Trust architecture follows three established principles: Verify explicitly Use least-privilege access Assume breach Azure supports these principles through several complementary security controls. Microsoft’s Zero Trust approach is comprehensive, but there are a few challenges: Applying Microsoft’s requirements is complicated in hybrid environments. To understand how least-privilege permissions are being used, security teams also need relevant activity monitoring, threat detection , and investigation evidence. Microsoft's assume-breach guidance for Azure calls for: Network segmentation Traffic visibility Threat detection Measures to limit the impact of a compromise Trusting Your Zero Trust Architecture with Fidelis Dynamic threat monitoring Proactive Cyber Defense Zero Trust in Action Read the Guide Why Authentication Alone Isn't Enough Microsoft Entra Conditional Access uses contextual signals to inform access decisions. Organizations can also enforce controls such as authentication strength requirements and device compliance. Microsoft’s Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) can respond to certain changes in identity or policy conditions for supported applications and resources. But access-policy evaluation and monitoring the behavior of an authenticated workload are different security functions. However, attackers may not need to bypass those controls directly. Activities that are particularly concerning are: A domain-joined Azure VM enumerating Active Directory objects or querying services over LDAP and Kerberos. An attacker reusing an approved administrative path to reach additional workloads or internal SMB shares. A compromised account accessing sensitive files within its assigned privileges. Unexpected outbound connections or data transfers over permitted channels. Workload configuration changes or service permission abuse intended to maintain access. Microsoft-native security tools can detect many of these behaviors when appropriately deployed and configured. Additional network inspection, deception , and workload monitoring can strengthen coverage. During an investigation, the SOC needs to connect the activity across systems. Without sufficient evidence, analysts may have several alerts but still struggle to establish the sequence and scope of the intrusion. At Fidelis, we address these requirements by strengthening the threat detection, investigation, and response capabilities that support an organization’s Azure Zero Trust strategy. How Fidelis Strengthens Azure Zero Trust Across Five Security Areas An effective Azure Zero Trust implementation depends on more than enforcing access decisions. Microsoft provides the identity, network, workload, and security operations controls needed to implement the architecture. At Fidelis, we strengthen the detection and investigation capabilities that support those controls, particularly when attackers exploit legitimate permissions or move across hybrid infrastructure. Our capabilities span: Network Inspection Traditional Active Directory threat detection Deception Cloud Security Posture Management Workload Protection Extended Detection and Response We focus on areas where security teams need to maintain visibility and investigate risk throughout the Azure Zero Trust architecture: Permitted network connections Hybrid identity infrastructure Attacker activity after compromise Cloud workload posture Coordinated detection and response Each addresses a different part of the Zero Trust strategy. Some help identify weaknesses that could undermine least privilege. Others support the assume-breach principle by detecting suspicious behavior and establishing the evidence needed for response. We complement Microsoft’s native security controls, giving organizations additional detection and investigation capabilities where their existing coverage needs greater depth. Here’s how our solutions contribute to an Azure Zero Trust architecture. 1. Monitor Activity Within Permitted Azure Network Connections Azure Zero Trust principle: Assume breach Network segmentation is an important part of Zero Trust in Azure. Organizations use NSGs, Azure Firewall, and other controls to restrict communication between workloads and networks. These controls help reduce unnecessary connectivity and limit potential lateral movement. Microsoft’s Azure Zero Trust networking guidance also calls for visibility into network traffic so organizations can detect threats within their infrastructure. However, attackers who have compromised an authorized workload may continue using the network paths already available to it. We address this challenge through Fidelis Network ® and our Deep Session Inspection ® (DSI) technology. DSI analyzes network sessions and extracts rich protocol-aware metadata, providing more context than connection-level flow records alone. We combine this information with threat intelligence to help security teams recognize suspicious activity. Fidelis Network ® helps analysts examine session behavior, identify unusual communication patterns, and investigate activity that could indicate reconnaissance or lateral movement, where relevant traffic is available to our sensors. This supports the assume-breach principle by adding threat detection within the network paths that an organization has deliberately permitted. It does not replace segmentation or make authorization decisions on Azure’s behalf. We also support preventative actions through appropriately configured sensor policies. When a detection rule is met and the applicable action is enabled, supported sensors can take action without requiring an analyst to manually initiate every response. Encrypted traffic requires a more nuanced approach. We can derive useful detection signals from TLS metadata and observable traffic characteristics without decrypting the payload. Where content inspection is necessary, we rely on supported decryption and inspection capabilities. There is also an architectural consideration specific to Azure. Our ability to analyze traffic depends on how it is made available to Fidelis sensors. We don’t assume that every Azure workload or managed service is automatically visible. During deployment, we recommend identifying the relevant Azure-to-on-premises and east-west traffic paths, confirming how traffic can be acquired through supported methods, and validating which sessions are visible to the sensors. For a Zero Trust deployment, this validation is essential as security teams need to know which permitted network paths are monitored, which services are outside the inspection scope, and where additional telemetry is necessary. Fidelis Network therefore contributes to Azure Zero Trust by helping organizations monitor permitted network activity, recognize suspicious behavior, and investigate possible lateral movement across supported network paths. 2. Detect Identity and Privilege Abuse Across Hybrid Environments Azure Zero Trust principles: Verify explicitly and use least privilege Identity remains central to Zero Trust, but we believe organizations need to distinguish between protecting cloud authentication and protecting traditional Active Directory infrastructure. Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure Active Directory, handles cloud identity and access management. Windows Server Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) continues to support domain authentication, Kerberos, LDAP, and other directory services used across enterprise networks. Azure Zero Trust relies on identity verification and least-privilege policies to control access to cloud resources. However, organizations with hybrid identity environments must also protect the traditional AD infrastructure that supports domain-connected workloads, applications, and administrative services. With Fidelis Active Directory Intercept , we combine AD-aware network inspection, directory-focused deception, and threat detection to identify suspicious behavior involving traditional Active Directory infrastructure. Our detection capabilities cover techniques such as: LDAP reconnaissance and AD enumeration. Kerberoasting and AS-REP roasting. Suspicious Kerberos authentication activity. DCSync and DCShadow. Lateral movement and privilege escalation involving AD infrastructure. We inspect relevant directory protocols and use deceptive AD objects and breadcrumbs to help identify attackers exploring the environment. This strengthens an Azure Zero Trust strategy by helping security teams identify attempts to abuse identities and privileges within traditional AD infrastructure. It complements Entra’s cloud identity controls rather than providing native Conditional Access enforcement. For organizations maintaining hybrid identity dependencies, enforcing least privilege reduces available permissions, while detecting attempts to misuse those permissions helps the SOC identify attacks that are already underway. 3. Use Deception to Expose Attackers After Access Is Granted Azure Zero Trust principle: Assume breach One difficulty with detecting attackers who have legitimate credentials is that their activity can resemble ordinary administration. Behavioral analytics can help distinguish suspicious activity, but analysts often need additional evidence before determining whether a particular action is malicious. We use deception to provide that evidence. Fidelis Deception ® places decoys, deceptive credentials, breadcrumbs, and other realistic assets in an organization’s environment. These assets are designed to be encountered by attackers conducting reconnaissance, searching for credentials, or attempting lateral movement. They have no legitimate production purpose. Unlike an ordinary connection to a production server, interaction with a properly configured deceptive asset has a much stronger implication of unauthorized activity. Microsoft’s assume-breach principle calls for security controls that operate with the expectation that attackers may already be present. Deception supports this objective by making certain post-compromise activities easier to identify. We also use cyber terrain mapping, asset discovery, and profiling to help determine where deceptive assets should be positioned. Placement is important. In Azure and hybrid deployments, Fidelis Deception can be used to strengthen detection around relevant workloads, identity infrastructure, and administrative access paths. The objective is not to deploy decoys indiscriminately. It is to place believable assets where attacker interaction would provide meaningful evidence and support earlier investigation. Fidelis Deception adds value to the assume-breach approach by helping identify attackers who are already operating within the environment, including those using compromised accounts or legitimate network paths. When integrated with our broader detection and response capabilities, deception alerts can also help analysts investigate the source of the activity and determine whether related reconnaissance or lateral movement occurred. 4. Continuously Assess Azure Workload Security and Risk Azure Zero Trust principles: Use least privilege and assume breach Azure Zero Trust also requires organizations to secure the infrastructure and workloads that users, applications, and services depend on. A workload can be properly authenticated and still introduce risk through insecure configurations, vulnerable software, or excessive permissions. These exposures can develop long after the workload was initially deployed. Microsoft recommends least-privilege permissions, secure workload configurations, network segmentation, and continuous security monitoring as part of Azure Zero Trust. Microsoft Defender for Cloud provides native cloud security posture management and workload protection. At Fidelis, we address these requirements through Fidelis Halo ® , which supports Azure as well as other cloud and on-premises environments. FIdelis Halo, our CNAPP, portfolio contributes to ongoing security posture assessment and workload monitoring through three services. These help security teams identify exposures and configuration changes that could undermine their Zero Trust objectives. 1. Fidelis Cloud Secure We provide agentless cloud security posture management to help organizations: Discover cloud resources Maintain inventory Assess configurations Identify security exposures Monitor compliance across supported Azure services In an Azure Zero Trust implementation, this supports the need to maintain awareness of cloud assets and the risks associated with their configurations. Consider an Azure workload deployed with unnecessary network exposure or permissions beyond its operational requirements. The access granted to that resource may be broader than the organization’s intended least-privilege model. Fidelis Cloud Secure can help identify supported configuration and permission-related risks so teams can investigate and remediate the exposure using the appropriate Azure controls. This is an important distinction. Fidelis Halo assesses relevant security risks; Azure’s native identity, authorization, and networking services remain responsible for enforcing their configured access policies. 2. Fidelis Server Secure We use lightweight microagents on supported Windows and Linux servers to monitor workload security . Capabilities include: Configuration assessment File integrity monitoring Log-based intrusion detection Vulnerability assessment Network connection visibility Consider an Azure VM supporting an important business application. An administrator modifies its configuration while troubleshooting an issue, unintentionally introducing a security weakness. Our workload monitoring capabilities can help identify relevant changes so the security team can investigate and remediate the exposure. From a Zero Trust perspective, the security posture of a workload cannot be assumed to remain unchanged after deployment. Configuration changes, new vulnerabilities , and unexpected host activity may alter the risk associated with that workload. Fidelis Server Secure provides workload-level findings that can help security teams identify these changes and assess whether further investigation or remediation is required. 3. Fidelis Container Secure We extend security assessment and monitoring to supported container environments, including container images, registries, hosts, and Kubernetes configurations. As organizations expand their containerized workloads, we help them assess vulnerabilities and configuration risks across the relevant infrastructure. In Azure environments using supported container infrastructure, these capabilities help teams assess security weaknesses across container images, hosts, and Kubernetes configurations. This supports the Zero Trust requirement to maintain secure infrastructure and reduce opportunities for attackers to exploit vulnerable or misconfigured workloads. We don’t believe organizations should add another cloud security product simply to produce more findings. If an organization already uses Defender for Cloud, we recommend evaluating Fidelis Halo against specific workload security and posture-management requirements. The strongest case for adding Fidelis is where it provides useful coverage or assessment capabilities across Azure, other cloud platforms, and on-premises infrastructure. For Azure Zero Trust, the contribution is better awareness of workload risk and configuration changes that could weaken the security controls organizations depend on. 5. Investigate and Respond When Authorized Access Is Misused Azure Zero Trust principle: Assume breach Microsoft’s Azure Zero Trust guidance includes continuous threat detection and response as part of the assume-breach approach. Segmentation helps limit the paths an attacker can use, while detection and investigation capabilities help determine whether a compromise has occurred and what systems may be affected. For a SOC investigating an attacker operating through legitimate access, the challenge is establishing what happened after the initial compromise. Was the compromised account used to access additional systems? Did the attacker reach sensitive information? Was data transferred outside an approved boundary? Our Fidelis Network Data Loss Prevention (DLP) capabilities use Deep Session Inspection and policy-based controls to identify sensitive content and potentially unauthorized data transfers within traffic available for inspection. For example, an attacker operating from a compromised Azure-connected workload may attempt to transfer protected information through an allowed communication channel. Where the traffic and content are available for inspection, Fidelis Network DLP can help identify transfers matching configured security policies and support investigation into possible data exfiltration. This complements Azure’s identity, network, and data protection controls by contributing detection and policy-based protection for sensitive information moving through monitored network paths. Detecting suspicious data movement is only part of an investigation. Analysts also need to understand the events leading up to it. We designed Fidelis Elevate ® , our open and active XDR platform, to bring supported network, endpoint, and deception capabilities together for detection, investigation, and coordinated response. Fidelis Network ® can provide session-level evidence. Fidelis Endpoint ® can contribute host and process information. Fidelis Deception ® can identify interactions with decoys and breadcrumbs. By correlating the available findings, we help analysts establish relationships between activity that might otherwise appear as separate events. Consider an incident involving a compromised Azure-hosted server. Network inspection identifies suspicious communication with an internal system. Endpoint telemetry reveals a process associated with the activity. A deception alert indicates that the same system attempted to interact with a decoy. When the relevant Fidelis capabilities are deployed and integrated, Fidelis Elevate can help analysts investigate these related findings, identify affected systems, and determine whether the activity represents a broader compromise. Where supported and properly configured, response can include endpoint containment, network prevention policies, and other coordinated actions. These capabilities support the assume-breach model by helping security teams move from suspicious activity to investigation and containment. Microsoft Entra ID, Azure networking services, and other native controls remain important for actions such as revoking access, modifying permissions, or restricting Azure resources. Our contribution is the additional threat context and supported response capabilities that help inform those decisions. Where Can Fidelis Add Value to Your Existing Azure Zero Trust Architecture? If your organization already uses Microsoft Entra ID, Defender for Cloud, Defender XDR, and Sentinel, evaluating Fidelis should begin with your existing Zero Trust coverage rather than a generic product comparison. We recommend looking at how effectively your current security stack supports the following requirements. 1. Visibility within segmented networks Azure NSGs and Azure Firewall help enforce network boundaries. But can your SOC investigate suspicious communications taking place through approved connections? Determine whether additional session-level evidence from Fidelis Network would improve detection and investigation. 2. Protection against identity and privilege abuse Conditional Access, Azure RBAC, and PIM support access control and least privilege. In hybrid environments, can your security team also detect attacks against traditional AD infrastructure? Evaluate Fidelis Active Directory Intercept against relevant Kerberos , LDAP, and credential-abuse scenarios. 3. Detection of attackers already inside the environment An assume-breach architecture should account for adversaries operating with compromised credentials or workloads. Assess whether Fidelis Deception can expose reconnaissance and lateral movement through realistic decoys and breadcrumbs placed along relevant attack paths. 4. Continuous workload risk assessment Azure Zero Trust depends on secure and appropriately configured workloads. Determine whether Fidelis Halo adds useful assessment or monitoring coverage for your Azure servers, containers, cloud resources, and hybrid infrastructure. Don’t let Threats go Unnoticed. See how Fidelis Elevate ® helps you: Identify and neutralize threats faster Gain full visibility across your attack surface Automate security operations for efficiency Download Now 5. Investigation and response across security domains Test whether your analysts can connect network, endpoint, and deception evidence during a simulated compromise. Evaluate how Fidelis Elevate contributes to the investigation and how its supported response capabilities work alongside your existing Microsoft security controls. We recommend testing these requirements using scenarios from your environment. For example, simulate suspicious AD enumeration from an Azure-hosted domain member or unusual SMB access through a permitted network connection. Include legitimate administrative activity so the evaluation can distinguish meaningful detections from unnecessary alerts. At Fidelis, we believe a Zero Trust investment should demonstrate an improvement in security outcomes. That could mean identifying activity that was previously difficult to detect, obtaining stronger investigation evidence, or improving the SOC’s ability to respond to a compromise. The objective is not to duplicate Microsoft’s access controls. It is to determine where our capabilities can make your existing Azure Zero Trust implementation more effective. Is Your Azure Zero Trust Strategy Ready for a Real Attack? It’s easy to measure how extensively you’ve implemented Azure security controls. You can review Conditional Access policies, audit permissions, check workload configurations, and assess compliance. But these assessments don’t always tell you how well your security team would handle an attacker operating across Azure and connected on-premises systems. At Fidelis, we believe organizations should judge their Azure Zero Trust maturity by what their security teams can actually establish during an incident, not just by the controls they have deployed. The next time you review your Azure Zero Trust architecture, consider this: If an attacker compromised one of your Azure workloads today, could your SOC trace where they went, what they accessed, and whether they reached systems beyond Azure? Frequently Asked Questions What is Azure Zero Trust security? Azure Zero Trust is Microsoft’s approach to securing identities, applications, workloads, networks, and data through explicit verification, least-privilege access, and an assume-breach strategy. It combines identity security and access enforcement with segmentation, monitoring, threat detection, and response. How does Azure Active Directory support Zero Trust? Azure Active Directory, now Microsoft Entra ID, supports Zero Trust through capabilities such as: Conditional Access Identity protection Privileged access management These help organizations manage access based on identity, device, risk, and other contextual signals. We complement these capabilities by helping detect suspicious activity within permitted network connections and traditional AD infrastructure. How does Fidelis help detect lateral movement in Azure and hybrid environments? We use Fidelis Network’s Deep Session Inspection and behavioral analytics to identify suspicious communication patterns in monitored traffic. Our Active Directory Intercept capabilities help identify directory-related attacks, while Fidelis Deception exposes attackers interacting with decoys and breadcrumbs. Together, these capabilities can strengthen lateral movement detection across supported Azure and hybrid network paths. Does Fidelis replace Microsoft Defender or Entra ID? No. We complement Microsoft’s native security capabilities. Microsoft Entra ID, Defender for Cloud, Defender XDR, and Sentinel provide identity protection, cloud security, detection, and investigation capabilities. We contribute additional network inspection, traditional AD threat detection, deception, workload assessment, and cross-domain investigation capabilities where organizations need them. Can Fidelis detect threats inside encrypted Azure traffic? We can analyze available TLS metadata and encrypted-traffic characteristics to identify suspicious patterns without necessarily decrypting the payload. Content-level inspection requires appropriate decryption and inspection capabilities. Actual visibility depends on the Azure network architecture and how relevant traffic is made available to Fidelis sensors. Citations: ^ 2026 Digital Defense Report
