items.title: Microsoft Teams Outage Hits Users in North America
items.summary: Microsoft is investigating a Microsoft Teams outage affecting users in North America, with automated recovery measures now reducing the disruption. The company is tracking the incident under TM1550488 in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Its latest supplied update indicates improvement, but does not confirm that service has fully returned. Microsoft’s initial notice said users were experiencing problems accessing Teams or using its features. The statement did not identify which functions were affected, how many organizations had reported problems, or whether the issue involved desktop, browser, or mobile clients. The reported scope remains North America, not a confirmed global outage. We're investigating reports of users experiencing issues when accessing or using Microsoft Teams functionality in North America, and more details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under TM1550488. — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 12, 2026 In a follow-up statement, Microsoft said it had “confirmed related impact scenarios” and updated the incident record. Its automated recovery features had taken action to restore service, while telemetry, the monitoring data used to track service behavior, showed those actions were reducing impact. Microsoft did not explain the recovery mechanism. We've confirmed related impact scenarios and have updated TM1550488. Our automated recovery features have taken action to restore service, and our telemetry indicates that these actions are effectively reducing impact. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center. — Microsoft 365 Status (@MSFT365Status) November 12, 2026 Falling impact does not establish that every affected user can access Teams normally. The supplied updates also provide no confirmed root cause, recovery deadline, or evidence linking the disruption to a cyberattack. Claims involving stolen data, malware, or account compromise would therefore be unsupported. The incident follows an earlier Microsoft Teams outage affecting United States users on October 26, tracked as TM1526111. Microsoft reported that automatic scaling restored that service. However, that earlier recovery does not establish what caused the current disruption or whether the same systems are involved. What Microsoft 365 Administrators Should Check Administrators should review TM1550488 through Health, then Service health, in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Microsoft’s service health guidance recommends checking for a known cloud incident before spending time on local troubleshooting. This helps teams separate a service problem from issues limited to their own environment. For support teams, the immediate task is to compare employee reports with the incident details available to their organization. Recording affected functions, error messages, locations, and failure times can help describe continuing problems clearly. The public notices alone are not detailed enough to justify naming individual Teams features as confirmed failures. Earlier Microsoft 365 service disruptions have affected Teams alongside other applications, including SharePoint and OneDrive. That history provides context, not proof of wider impact today. The current notices identify Teams, so extending the incident to Exchange Online, Outlook, or other Microsoft services would go beyond the available evidence. The latest supplied position is that automated recovery is reducing impact while TM1550488 remains the reference for further details. Organizations should distinguish that progress from confirmed closure. Microsoft’s service health dashboard provides incident updates and a history of resolved issues, allowing administrators to verify when the company formally reports restoration for their affected environment. items.title: When Attackers Move at AI Speed, How Can Your SOC Keep Up?
items.summary: Artificial intelligence is changing the cybersecurity landscape at an unprecedented pace. While enterprises are using AI to improve efficiency, cybercriminals are finding new ways to automate attacks, refine phishing campaigns, and scale their operations. What once required significant time and technical expertise can now be accomplished faster and with fewer resources. For SOC and MSSP teams, this means more suspicious activity to investigate, more indicators to validate, and growing pressure to distinguish genuine threats from background noise. The challenge is particularly relevant for organizations in the United States and Europe, which remain among the most targeted markets for cyberattacks. As attackers become faster and more adaptable, security teams face an uncomfortable reality: H ow do you investigate threats effectively when the time available to understand them keeps shrinking? A Growing Threat Landscape: Why the US and Europe Need to Stay Alert The United States and Europe remain major targets of cybercrime, ransomware, and attacks against critical infrastructure. Recent government reports highlight the scale of the challenge. The FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report, released in April 2026, recorded over $20 billion in reported internet crime losses in the US, a 26% increase from 2024. More than one million complaints were filed, with phishing, spoofing, and extortion among the most common. In Europe, ENISA’s 2026 Threat Landscape identifies ransomware as the EU’s most impactful cyber threat, with public administration among the most targeted sectors. CERT-EU also reported an increase in threat actors targeting EU institutions and their ecosystem, from 110 in 2024 to 174 in 2025, highlighting increasingly sophisticated social engineering, including AI-generated phishing and deepfakes. For enterprises, the implications are clear: attackers are becoming more adaptable, while security teams face growing volumes of suspicious activity and less time to investigate. SOCs and MSSPs need to do more than detect attacks to stay ahead. They must understand suspicious indicators, connect related threats, and find reliable answers before incidents escalate. The Investigation Bottleneck: Getting Answers Before Threats Escalate For SOC analysts, identifying a suspicious indicator is often just the start of an investigation. An unfamiliar IP appears in network logs. An employee receives an unexpected attachment. A security tool flags a potentially malicious URL. Each alert raises familiar questions: Is it malicious? Has it appeared in previous attacks? Is it linked to a known threat actor or campaign? And what should happen next? Without enough context, analysts can lose valuable time switching between tools, checking intelligence sources, and correlating findings manually. The challenge is even greater for MSSPs investigating activity across multiple customer environments. High alert volumes and the need to validate indicators individually can quickly create operational bottlenecks. ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Lookup helps accelerate these investigations. By searching suspicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, analysts can quickly assess reputation and access available intelligence, including malicious classifications, related threats, and historical observations. Rather than starting from scratch, they can use existing context to guide their investigation. Get threat context in 2 seconds to validate indicators and accelerate your investigations. Power Up Your SOC For example, a lookup on an IP associated with suspicious outbound traffic may reveal previous malicious activity or links to known campaigns. This helps analysts prioritize alerts and determine where to focus their efforts. Uncovering malicious indicators associated with the selected IP in TI Lookup Still, reputation alone cannot establish whether an indicator is malicious. A newly registered domain may have no history, while a suspicious file may require deeper analysis. TI Lookup is therefore a starting point for investigation, not a final verdict. Beyond the Indicator: Understanding What a Threat Actually Does Knowing that a file or URL is suspicious is useful. Understanding its behavior is even more valuable. Static indicators provide an initial assessment, but they don’t reveal what happens when a file executes or a URL is accessed. Does it establish persistence, communicate with external infrastructure, or download additional payloads? These details help analysts assess a threat’s potential impact. An interactive sandbox like the one offered by ANY.RUN provides a controlled environment to analyze suspicious files and URLs, observe execution behavior, and investigate network communications without exposing production systems. Detonating a ZIP archive containing the Formbook infection in ANY.RUN Sandbox Connecting sandbox analysis with Threat Intelligence Lookup adds another layer of context. The powerful new capability called R elated Threat Context presented in ANY.RUN’s sandbox helps analysts explore connected threat activity and related analyses, linking observed behavior to known indicators, campaigns, and malicious infrastructure. By investigating suspicious IPs or domains identified during execution, analysts can uncover additional connections and potential threats that might otherwise go unnoticed. Exploring the Related Threat Context capability in ANY.RUN’s Sandbox For SOC teams, it means deeper investigations and better-informed decisions. And for MSSPs , it provides additional context across customer environments. The goal is not just to confirm malicious activity, but to understand how a threat operates and what analysts should investigate next. Uncover up to 24x more IOCs per case and gain deeper insight into connected threats and malicious infrastructure. Accelerate Your SOC Staying Ahead, Not Just Catching Up: The Importance of Continuous Threat Intelligence Even a thorough investigation provides only a snapshot of a constantly changing threat landscape. Malicious domains emerge, infrastructure gets replaced, and threat actors adapt. Intelligence that was relevant yesterday may not be enough for tomorrow’s investigations. Threat intelligence feeds help SOC and MSSP teams keep pace by providing continuously updated information on malicious IPs, domains, URLs, file hashes, and emerging threats. Fresh intelligence can help analysts recognize suspicious activity earlier and enrich investigations without relying entirely on manual lookups. For instance, ANY.RUN ’s internal analysis found that up to 30% of unique malicious indicators observed in Interactive Sandbox sessions had already been identified by ANY.RUN and were available in Threat Intelligence Feeds . ANY.RUN TI Feeds give SOCs & MSSPs access to live threat intel on current attacks This finding highlights the practical value of continuously updated intelligence: when these indicators appear in an organization’s telemetry, security systems can potentially match them against TI Feeds before analysts begin a manual sandbox investigation. This gives SOC teams an opportunity to identify known malicious activity earlier and prioritize their response. Continuously updated feeds also help MSSPs monitor multiple customer environments and maintain visibility into emerging threats. Turning Threat Intelligence into an Everyday SOC Advantage Having access to threat intelligence is one thing. Making it useful across everyday security operations is another. SOC teams need to connect intelligence gathering, investigation, and response without adding complexity. Indicators flagged during routine monitoring should be easy to investigate, enrich with context, and escalate when necessary. A practical workflow can bring these capabilities together: Check indicators with TI Lookup: Investigate suspicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes to establish their reputation and identify known malicious associations. Dig deeper with sandboxing: When an indicator requires further examination, analyze suspicious files or URLs in an interactive sandbox. Explore execution behavior and related threat context to uncover additional indicators and potential attack connections. Keep intelligence current: Use threat intelligence feeds to stay informed about emerging malicious infrastructure, campaigns, and indicators that may affect the organization or its customers. Make informed decisions: Combine lookup results, behavioral analysis, and updated intelligence to prioritize investigations and determine appropriate response actions. For MSSPs , this approach can also help standardize investigation processes across multiple customer environments. Analysts gain a more consistent way to validate indicators, investigate suspicious activity, and work with relevant threat context, even when managing high volumes of alerts. Cut MTTR by 21 minutes and give your SOC the context to investigate and respond faster. Explore for Your Team Conclusion AI will continue to change the speed and scale of cyberattacks, and security teams shouldn’t expect the pressure on their operations to ease. For enterprises in the US and EU, maintaining strong security visibility requires more than simply detecting suspicious activity. It requires understanding what lies behind it. Behavior analysis and continuously updated threat intelligence give SOC and MSSP analysts different but complementary ways to investigate threats, uncover context, and make informed decisions. Attackers may be moving at AI speed, but with the right intelligence and investigation capabilities, your SOC doesn’t have to fall behind.

Each alert raises familiar questions: Is it malicious? Has it appeared in previous attacks? Is it linked to a known threat actor or campaign? And what should happen next? 

Without enough context, analysts can lose valuable time switching between tools, checking intelligence sources, and correlating findings manually. 

The challenge is even greater for MSSPs investigating activity across multiple customer environments. High alert volumes and the need to validate indicators individually can quickly create operational bottlenecks. 

ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Lookup helps accelerate these investigations. 

By searching suspicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, analysts can quickly assess reputation and access available intelligence, including malicious classifications, related threats, and historical observations.

Rather than starting from scratch, they can use existing context to guide their investigation. 

Get threat context in 2 seconds to validate indicators and accelerate your investigations. Power Up Your SOC 

For example, a lookup on an IP associated with suspicious outbound traffic may reveal previous malicious activity or links to known campaigns. This helps analysts prioritize alerts and determine where to focus their efforts. 

Uncovering malicious indicators associated with the selected IP in TI Lookup 

Still, reputation alone cannot establish whether an indicator is malicious. A newly registered domain may have no history, while a suspicious file may require deeper analysis. TI Lookup is therefore a starting point for investigation, not a final verdict.  

Beyond the Indicator: Understanding What a Threat Actually Does 

Knowing that a file or URL is suspicious is useful. Understanding its behavior is even more valuable. 

Static indicators provide an initial assessment, but they don’t reveal what happens when a file executes or a URL is accessed.

Does it establish persistence, communicate with external infrastructure, or download additional payloads? These details help analysts assess a threat’s potential impact. 

An interactive sandbox like the one offered by ANY.RUN provides a controlled environment to analyze suspicious files and URLs, observe execution behavior, and investigate network communications without exposing production systems. 

Detonating a ZIP archive containing the Formbook infection in ANY.RUN Sandbox 

Connecting sandbox analysis with Threat Intelligence Lookup adds another layer of context. The powerful new capability called Related Threat Context presented in ANY.RUN’s sandbox helps analysts explore connected threat activity and related analyses, linking observed behavior to known indicators, campaigns, and malicious infrastructure.

By investigating suspicious IPs or domains identified during execution, analysts can uncover additional connections and potential threats that might otherwise go unnoticed. 

Exploring the Related Threat Context capability in ANY.RUN’s Sandbox 

For SOC teams, it means deeper investigations and better-informed decisions. And for MSSPs, it provides additional context across customer environments. 

The goal is not just to confirm malicious activity, but to understand how a threat operates and what analysts should investigate next. 

Uncover up to 24x more IOCs per case and gain deeper insight into connected threats and malicious infrastructure. Accelerate Your SOC 

Staying Ahead, Not Just Catching Up: The Importance of Continuous Threat Intelligence 

Even a thorough investigation provides only a snapshot of a constantly changing threat landscape. Malicious domains emerge, infrastructure gets replaced, and threat actors adapt.

Intelligence that was relevant yesterday may not be enough for tomorrow’s investigations. 

Threat intelligence feeds help SOC and MSSP teams keep pace by providing continuously updated information on malicious IPs, domains, URLs, file hashes, and emerging threats.

Fresh intelligence can help analysts recognize suspicious activity earlier and enrich investigations without relying entirely on manual lookups. 

For instance, ANY.RUN’s internal analysis found that up to 30% of unique malicious indicators observed in Interactive Sandbox sessions had already been identified by ANY.RUN and were available in Threat Intelligence Feeds. 

ANY.RUN TI Feeds give SOCs & MSSPs access to live threat intel on current attacks 

This finding highlights the practical value of continuously updated intelligence: when these indicators appear in an organization’s telemetry, security systems can potentially match them against TI Feeds before analysts begin a manual sandbox investigation.

This gives SOC teams an opportunity to identify known malicious activity earlier and prioritize their response. 

Continuously updated feeds also help MSSPs monitor multiple customer environments and maintain visibility into emerging threats. 

Turning Threat Intelligence into an Everyday SOC Advantage 

Having access to threat intelligence is one thing. Making it useful across everyday security operations is another. 

SOC teams need to connect intelligence gathering, investigation, and response without adding complexity. Indicators flagged during routine monitoring should be easy to investigate, enrich with context, and escalate when necessary. 

A practical workflow can bring these capabilities together: 

  • Check indicators with TI Lookup: Investigate suspicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes to establish their reputation and identify known malicious associations. 
  • Dig deeper with sandboxing: When an indicator requires further examination, analyze suspicious files or URLs in an interactive sandbox. Explore execution behavior and related threat context to uncover additional indicators and potential attack connections. 
  • Keep intelligence current: Use threat intelligence feeds to stay informed about emerging malicious infrastructure, campaigns, and indicators that may affect the organization or its customers. 
  • Make informed decisions: Combine lookup results, behavioral analysis, and updated intelligence to prioritize investigations and determine appropriate response actions. 

For MSSPs, this approach can also help standardize investigation processes across multiple customer environments.

Analysts gain a more consistent way to validate indicators, investigate suspicious activity, and work with relevant threat context, even when managing high volumes of alerts. 

Cut MTTR by 21 minutes and give your SOC the context to investigate and respond faster. Explore for Your Team 

Conclusion 

AI will continue to change the speed and scale of cyberattacks, and security teams shouldn’t expect the pressure on their operations to ease.

For enterprises in the US and EU, maintaining strong security visibility requires more than simply detecting suspicious activity. It requires understanding what lies behind it. 

Behavior analysis and continuously updated threat intelligence give SOC and MSSP analysts different but complementary ways to investigate threats, uncover context, and make informed decisions. 

Attackers may be moving at AI speed, but with the right intelligence and investigation capabilities, your SOC doesn’t have to fall behind.

CNCF Recognizes Cloud Native Champions in 2026 Community Awards
items.summary: Annual awards honor leaders, maintainers, and documentarians building open source infrastructure Key Highlights CNCF recognized 11 contributors across four Community Awards at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City, with winners honored at the November 12 ceremony. Lifetime Achievement honorees Julius Volz, co-creator of Prometheus, and Rita Zhang, chair of Kubernetes SIG Auth, spent over a decade building the observability and security foundations the community relies on to meet two of its biggest challenges in the age of AI. Top Committer Antonio Ojea advanced Kubernetes networking and testing, from IPv6 dual-stack support to DRANET, which extends Dynamic Resource Allocation to network resources. From Istio release engineering and core Kubernetes controllers to documentation for Kubernetes, HAMi, Cilium, and eBPF, this year’s winners highlight the behind-the-scenes work that keeps projects dependable as organizations scale AI and cloud native workloads. KUBECON + CLOUDNATIVECON NORTH AMERICA, SALT LAKE CITY – November 12, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced the winners of the CNCF Community Awards at the annual KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America . Since 2016, the CNCF Community Awards celebrate key contributors across CNCF projects and Technical Advisory Groups (TAGs). These awards honor leaders committed to the cloud native ecosystem, maintainers dedicated to the vitality of their projects, documentarians who enhance usability, and behind-the-scenes contributors essential to our community. Winners were recognized and received their trophies during the event’s award ceremony. “This year’s award recipients show what it takes to keep this community running year after year,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “From maintaining critical infrastructure, security updates, to writing the docs that make projects usable, to showing up for their local communities, these contributors do the gritty work that keeps our projects dependable. Thank you to every winner for the care they bring to the community.” Lifetime Achievement Award The Lifetime Achievement Award is presented to longtime contributors who have significantly influenced cloud native technologies and demonstrated sustained commitment to the ecosystem. This award honors individuals whose efforts over the past decade have been instrumental in shaping and supporting the Kubernetes and CNCF communities. This year’s recipients built tools the community relies on to meet two of its biggest challenges in the age of AI: seeing what’s running in production, and securing and governing it. This event’s recipients are: Julius Volz ( juliusv ) Rita Zhang ( ritazh ) “The Lifetime Achievement Award honors the people whose sustained work keeps this community strong and moving forward,” said Jonathan Bryce, CNCF Executive Director. “Julius Volz and Rita Zhang spent over a decade building the observability and security infrastructure this community depends on every day. From Prometheus to Kubernetes security tooling, their work ensures the enduring health of the entire cloud native community for years to come.” Top Committer Award The Top Committer Award, also known as the Top Cloud Native Committer Award, recognizes an individual for incredible technical skills and notable achievements across one or more CNCF projects as a maintainer. This accolade highlights sustained, collaborative development that benefits CNCF-hosted projects as a whole. The award honors those who demonstrate deep technical impact whose work reflects dedicated contributions essential for the ongoing vitality of the cloud native ecosystem. This year’s winner has advanced Kubernetes networking and testing, from IPv6 dual-stack support and the KIND testing infrastructure to DRANET, which extends Dynamic Resource Allocation, Kubernetes’ way of assigning specialized hardware, to network resources. This event’s winner is: Antonio Ojea ( aojea ) Chop Wood Carry Water Award The Chop Wood Carry Water Award recognizes the essential, behind-the-scenes community work that keeps the cloud native ecosystem healthy and long-lived. This accolade honors contributors who spend countless hours completing often mundane but critical tasks, such as supporting documentation, organizing meetups, and maintaining project infrastructure. This year’s winners include contributors who manage Istio releases and infrastructure, maintain core Kubernetes controllers, and lead community mentorship across projects. This event’s winners are: Maciej Szulik ( soltysh ) Saiyam Pathak ( saiyam1814 ) Steven Jin ( Stevenjin8 ) Francisco Herrera ( fjglira ) Joe Stringer ( joestringer ) Lorem Ipsum The Lorem Ipsum award, previously known as the Top Documentarian award, recognizes excellence in documentation contributions made to the CNCF and its hosted projects. Recipients are honored for their efforts to enhance usability and inclusion across CNCF projects. This year’s winners maintain and improve documentation for Kubernetes, HAMi, Cilium, and the eBPF ecosystem. This event’s winners are: Natali Vlatko ( natalisucks ) Jimmy Song ( rootsongjc ) Dylan Reimerink ( dylandreimerink ) CNCF encourages the community to participate in ongoing initiatives that strengthen the cloud native ecosystem. Technologists are invited to join the CNCF End User Community to collaborate with peers and contribute to the influential group of organizations harnessing cloud native architectures to solve real-world problems. Check the CNCF calendar for details on local events and register for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe . About Cloud Native Computing Foundation Cloud native computing empowers organizations to build and run scalable applications with an open source software stack in public, private, and hybrid clouds. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) hosts critical components of the global technology infrastructure, including Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy. CNCF brings together the industry’s top developers, end users, and vendors and runs the largest open source developer conferences in the world. Supported by nearly 800 members, including the world’s largest cloud computing and software companies, as well as over 200 innovative startups, CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation. For more information, please visit www.cncf.io . Media Contact The Linux Foundation pr@cncf.io

items.title: CVE-2026-119618: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Enables Remote Code Execution
items.summary: Apache has released an urgent security update addressing CVE-2026-119618, a critical remote code execution vulnerability in the mod_http2 module of Apache HTTP Server. The flaw affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to corrupt heap memory and potentially execute arbitrary commands on vulnerable servers. The vulnerability stems from improper synchronization when Apache processes concurrent HTTP/2 requests. Multiple threads can access shared resources without sufficient coordination, creating a race condition that allows one thread to modify memory being used by another. Successful exploitation can corrupt the server’s internal heap and ultimately lead to remote code execution. Only Apache deployments with HTTP/2 enabled are exposed to the known attack path. Servers configured exclusively for HTTP/1.1 do not reach the vulnerable mod_http2 functionality. HTTP/2 can be enabled using h2 for TLS connections or h2c for cleartext HTTP/2 through Apache’s Protocols directive. Contact Sales Apache addressed the vulnerability in HTTP Server 2.4.71, released on November 11, 2026. Standalone releases of mod_h2 from GitHub versions 2.0.8 through 2.0.42 are also affected. Apache’s official advisory does not currently identify a separately released fixed standalone mod_h2 version. Red Hat has assigned the vulnerability a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 for its general assessment, with network-accessible, low-complexity exploitation requiring neither authentication nor user interaction. Red Hat further states that research has demonstrated reliable exploitation against a default-configured server with mod_http2 enabled. However, as of November 12, 2026, neither Apache nor the reviewed security reports document exploitation in real-world attacks. Wiz likewise reported no known in-the-wild exploitation at publication time. Organizations should nevertheless prioritize remediation because the vulnerability is remotely reachable and its technical root cause is now public. Organizations can strengthen defenses against emerging exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, enabling security teams to operationalize threat intelligence and accelerate detection engineering and threat hunting across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Detect CVE-2026-119618 by identifying vulnerable internet-facing Apache servers with HTTP/2 enabled and correlating suspicious HTTP/2 activity with Apache crashes, abnormal child processes, unexpected command execution, newly created files, and unusual outbound network connections. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. CVE-2026-119618 analysis CVE-2026-119618 affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when the vulnerable mod_http2 functionality is present and HTTP/2 is enabled. The standalone mod_h2 project is affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. Apache classifies the issue as critical and maps it to CWE-362, Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization. The vulnerability exists in the assign_headers() function used by Apache’s HTTP/2 processing. HTTP/2 differs significantly from HTTP/1.1 because multiple streams can operate concurrently over a single connection. Apache’s mod_http2 module therefore uses several threads to process requests and manage HTTP/2 streams simultaneously. The problem occurs when these threads interact with shared memory without sufficient synchronization. According to Red Hat’s technical assessment, an HTTP/2 stream worker can write into memory owned by the connection thread through a shared, lock-free allocator. Under attacker-controlled timing, concurrent access can corrupt the heap. Heap corruption vulnerabilities can have different outcomes depending on memory layout and attacker control. Failed exploitation may cause Apache worker processes to crash, while a sufficiently controlled corruption can modify program state or redirect execution. Red Hat states that successful exploitation can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the Apache HTTP Server process. This can give attackers access to application data, configuration files, credentials available to the web server, and other resources accessible under that security context. The vulnerability is particularly concerning on internet-facing systems because no valid account, password, API key, or other authentication is required. An attacker only needs network access to an affected HTTP/2 endpoint. Exposure nevertheless depends on configuration. Apache HTTP Server must actually offer HTTP/2. Administrators can enable this through the Protocols directive using: Protocols h2 http/1.1 for HTTP/2 over TLS, or: Protocols h2c http/1.1 where cleartext HTTP/2 is supported. The directive can be configured globally or on individual virtual hosts, meaning administrators should inspect both server-wide and per-site configurations when assessing exposure. A server that runs an affected Apache version but serves only HTTP/1.1 is not vulnerable through this flaw. Red Hat specifically confirms that systems without HTTP/2 enabled do not reach the affected code path. Apache’s upstream affected range should also not be applied blindly to Linux distribution packages. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and earlier releases do not contain the vulnerable code and are not affected. RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 do include affected mod_http2 packages, but Red Hat rates the issue Important rather than Critical on those platforms. The difference comes from implementation details. On RHEL 9 and 10, each HTTP/2 stream receives a separate memory allocator rather than sharing the same allocator with the connection. Red Hat states that this architecture substantially increases exploitation complexity, although affected systems still require security updates. Red Hat released corrected packages for multiple RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 streams on November 11. Administrators using vendor-maintained Linux packages should apply their distribution’s security update instead of determining vulnerability solely from the upstream Apache version displayed by the server. Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 provides the upstream correction. The fix modifies the vulnerable synchronization and memory-management behavior so that concurrent HTTP/2 operations cannot interact with the affected shared resources in the unsafe manner. The vulnerability was independently discovered through two research efforts. Anthropic’s OSS Scanner reported the issue to Apache’s security team on October 26, 2026 under identifier ANT-2026-MAPKT6MZ. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research independently reported the vulnerability on November 3. Apache released the fix on November 11. The CVE record was published on November 11, 2026. The CVE-2026-119618 PoC situation requires careful interpretation. Red Hat states that public research demonstrated a reliable exploit against a default-configured server with mod_http2 enabled. However, The Hacker News and Wiz reported that no publicly available RCE exploit had been identified when their reports were published. Public GitHub projects claiming scanners or exploitation-related tooling should therefore not automatically be interpreted as validated weaponized RCE code. This distinction matters operationally. Defenders should assume the flaw is technically exploitable while avoiding claims that a reliable weaponized exploit is already circulating broadly unless further evidence emerges. For CVE-2026-119618 detection, security teams should first identify exposed systems rather than relying only on exploit signatures. Administrators can confirm whether the HTTP/2 module is loaded using: apachectl -M | grep http2 They should then inspect Apache configuration files for Protocols directives containing h2 or h2c, including directives defined inside individual virtual hosts. External service discovery can also identify servers negotiating HTTP/2 through TLS ALPN. However, version identification alone can be misleading because Linux distributions frequently backport vulnerability fixes without changing the upstream-looking version string. Runtime telemetry should be correlated with suspicious HTTP/2 traffic. Potential behavioral indicators include repeated Apache worker crashes, segmentation faults, abnormal restarts, memory-corruption messages, or sudden service instability associated with unusual HTTP/2 request bursts. Because successful exploitation can provide command execution, endpoint and host telemetry should also be reviewed for unusual child processes originating from Apache. Examples include httpd or apache2 unexpectedly launching shells, scripting interpreters, download utilities, or system administration commands. Security teams should investigate process relationships such as: httpd → /bin/sh apache2 → bash httpd → curl apache2 → wget or other execution chains inconsistent with the hosted application’s normal behavior. File creation within temporary directories, web roots, startup locations, or writable application folders can also indicate post-exploitation activity. Unexpected outbound connections from Apache worker processes should receive similar scrutiny. There are currently no vendor-published campaign-specific CVE-2026-119618 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or attacker infrastructure because Apache and the reviewed sources have not reported exploitation in the wild. This makes configuration assessment and behavior-based monitoring more valuable than static indicator matching. CVE-2026-119618 Mitigation The primary remediation is to upgrade affected Apache HTTP Server installations to version 2.4.71 or apply the corrected security package supplied by the operating system vendor. Apache 2.4.71 was released on November 11, 2026 and contains the upstream fix. Organizations should prioritize internet-facing Apache deployments with HTTP/2 enabled because these systems expose the vulnerable functionality directly to untrusted network traffic. Administrators should take the following steps: Inventory Apache HTTP Server deployments across production, development, cloud, and container environments. Identify installations running Apache 2.4.55 through 2.4.70. Verify whether mod_http2 is loaded. Inspect global and virtual-host Protocols directives for h2 or h2c. Upgrade upstream Apache deployments to 2.4.71 or later. Apply distribution-specific packages when Apache is managed through Debian, Red Hat, Amazon Linux, or another operating system vendor. Restart Apache after patching to ensure vulnerable worker processes are no longer running. Verify the effective HTTP server configuration after remediation. Review historical telemetry for suspicious activity on internet-facing systems that were exposed before patching. Administrators should not assume that installing an operating system package with a version number below 2.4.71 means the system remains vulnerable. Vendors such as Red Hat backport security fixes into their own package versions, so the relevant distribution advisory should be treated as authoritative. The official Apache advisory does not provide a workaround. However, organizations that cannot patch immediately can temporarily remove HTTP/2 from exposed configurations, eliminating access to the known vulnerable code path. Wiz recommends restricting the server to HTTP/1.1 until the update can be deployed. For example: Protocols http/1.1 Organizations applying this workaround should inspect all virtual hosts because a site-specific configuration can independently enable h2 or h2c. Removing HTTP/2 can affect application performance and client behavior, so the change should be tested and treated as a temporary risk-reduction measure rather than a replacement for installing the security update. The CVE-2026-119618 mitigation strategy should also include reducing unnecessary exposure. Administrative or internal Apache services that do not need direct internet connectivity should be restricted through network segmentation, load balancers, reverse proxies, firewall policies, or private addressing. Organizations using standalone mod_h2 releases between 2.0.8 and 2.0.42 require particular attention. Apache identifies those releases as affected, while The Hacker News reported that no corrected standalone release had been published at the time of its November 12 report. Disabling HTTP/2 or migrating to an Apache HTTP Server package containing the upstream fix may therefore be necessary until an appropriate standalone update is available. If suspicious activity is discovered, defenders should isolate the affected server where operationally feasible and preserve Apache access logs, error logs, system logs, process telemetry, network connections, and relevant memory or crash information. Successful exploitation should be treated as potential server compromise rather than simply a service crash. Investigators should look for new files, webshells, altered application code, persistence mechanisms, stolen credentials, suspicious outbound traffic, and evidence of lateral movement. Credentials accessible to the Apache process, including database passwords, API keys, cloud credentials, TLS private keys, or secrets stored in application configuration, should be reviewed and rotated when evidence suggests attacker-controlled code execution occurred. FAQ What is CVE-2026-119618 and how does it work? CVE-2026-119618 is a critical race condition in Apache HTTP Server’s mod_http2 module. Concurrent HTTP/2 processing can cause multiple threads to access shared memory without proper synchronization, resulting in heap corruption. A remote unauthenticated attacker who can reach an affected HTTP/2 service may be able to manipulate this corruption and execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the Apache server process. When was CVE-2026-119618 first discovered? Anthropic’s OSS Scanner reported the flaw to Apache on October 26, 2026. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research independently reported it on November 3. Apache publicly disclosed the vulnerability and released Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 containing the fix on November 11, 2026. What is the impact of CVE-2026-119618 on systems? Successful exploitation can corrupt Apache’s heap and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. An attacker may execute commands using the privileges of the Apache process, potentially access sensitive application data, modify files, establish persistence, disrupt services, or use the compromised server as an entry point for further attacks. Red Hat assigns the flaw a generic CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8. Can CVE-2026-119618 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 remain vulnerable when mod_http2 and HTTP/2 are enabled unless the operating system vendor has backported the fix. As of November 12, 2026, the reviewed sources do not report confirmed exploitation in the wild, but reliable exploitation has been demonstrated in security research. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-119618? Upgrade upstream Apache HTTP Server to 2.4.71 or later, or install the fixed package supplied by your Linux distribution. If immediate patching is impossible, temporarily disable HTTP/2 by removing h2 and h2c from the Protocols configuration and restrict unnecessary external access. Security teams should monitor Apache’s advisory and distribution security trackers for updated details for CVE-2026-119618 as additional exploit research and remediation information becomes available.

Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added.

CVE-2026-119618 analysis

CVE-2026-119618 affects Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 when the vulnerable mod_http2 functionality is present and HTTP/2 is enabled. The standalone mod_h2 project is affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. Apache classifies the issue as critical and maps it to CWE-362, Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization.

The vulnerability exists in the assign_headers() function used by Apache’s HTTP/2 processing.

HTTP/2 differs significantly from HTTP/1.1 because multiple streams can operate concurrently over a single connection. Apache’s mod_http2 module therefore uses several threads to process requests and manage HTTP/2 streams simultaneously.

The problem occurs when these threads interact with shared memory without sufficient synchronization. According to Red Hat’s technical assessment, an HTTP/2 stream worker can write into memory owned by the connection thread through a shared, lock-free allocator.

Under attacker-controlled timing, concurrent access can corrupt the heap.

Heap corruption vulnerabilities can have different outcomes depending on memory layout and attacker control. Failed exploitation may cause Apache worker processes to crash, while a sufficiently controlled corruption can modify program state or redirect execution.

Red Hat states that successful exploitation can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the Apache HTTP Server process. This can give attackers access to application data, configuration files, credentials available to the web server, and other resources accessible under that security context.

The vulnerability is particularly concerning on internet-facing systems because no valid account, password, API key, or other authentication is required. An attacker only needs network access to an affected HTTP/2 endpoint.

Exposure nevertheless depends on configuration.

Apache HTTP Server must actually offer HTTP/2. Administrators can enable this through the Protocols directive using:

Protocols h2 http/1.1

for HTTP/2 over TLS, or:

Protocols h2c http/1.1

where cleartext HTTP/2 is supported.

The directive can be configured globally or on individual virtual hosts, meaning administrators should inspect both server-wide and per-site configurations when assessing exposure.

A server that runs an affected Apache version but serves only HTTP/1.1 is not vulnerable through this flaw. Red Hat specifically confirms that systems without HTTP/2 enabled do not reach the affected code path.

Apache’s upstream affected range should also not be applied blindly to Linux distribution packages.

Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and earlier releases do not contain the vulnerable code and are not affected. RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 do include affected mod_http2 packages, but Red Hat rates the issue Important rather than Critical on those platforms.

The difference comes from implementation details. On RHEL 9 and 10, each HTTP/2 stream receives a separate memory allocator rather than sharing the same allocator with the connection. Red Hat states that this architecture substantially increases exploitation complexity, although affected systems still require security updates.

Red Hat released corrected packages for multiple RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 streams on November 11. Administrators using vendor-maintained Linux packages should apply their distribution’s security update instead of determining vulnerability solely from the upstream Apache version displayed by the server.

Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 provides the upstream correction. The fix modifies the vulnerable synchronization and memory-management behavior so that concurrent HTTP/2 operations cannot interact with the affected shared resources in the unsafe manner.

The vulnerability was independently discovered through two research efforts.

Anthropic’s OSS Scanner reported the issue to Apache’s security team on October 26, 2026 under identifier ANT-2026-MAPKT6MZ. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research independently reported the vulnerability on November 3. Apache released the fix on November 11.

The CVE record was published on November 11, 2026.

The CVE-2026-119618 PoC situation requires careful interpretation. Red Hat states that public research demonstrated a reliable exploit against a default-configured server with mod_http2 enabled. However, The Hacker News and Wiz reported that no publicly available RCE exploit had been identified when their reports were published. Public GitHub projects claiming scanners or exploitation-related tooling should therefore not automatically be interpreted as validated weaponized RCE code.

This distinction matters operationally. Defenders should assume the flaw is technically exploitable while avoiding claims that a reliable weaponized exploit is already circulating broadly unless further evidence emerges.

For CVE-2026-119618 detection, security teams should first identify exposed systems rather than relying only on exploit signatures.

Administrators can confirm whether the HTTP/2 module is loaded using:

apachectl -M | grep http2

They should then inspect Apache configuration files for Protocols directives containing h2 or h2c, including directives defined inside individual virtual hosts.

External service discovery can also identify servers negotiating HTTP/2 through TLS ALPN. However, version identification alone can be misleading because Linux distributions frequently backport vulnerability fixes without changing the upstream-looking version string.

Runtime telemetry should be correlated with suspicious HTTP/2 traffic. Potential behavioral indicators include repeated Apache worker crashes, segmentation faults, abnormal restarts, memory-corruption messages, or sudden service instability associated with unusual HTTP/2 request bursts.

Because successful exploitation can provide command execution, endpoint and host telemetry should also be reviewed for unusual child processes originating from Apache.

Examples include httpd or apache2 unexpectedly launching shells, scripting interpreters, download utilities, or system administration commands.

Security teams should investigate process relationships such as:

httpd → /bin/sh

apache2 → bash

httpd → curl

apache2 → wget

or other execution chains inconsistent with the hosted application’s normal behavior.

File creation within temporary directories, web roots, startup locations, or writable application folders can also indicate post-exploitation activity. Unexpected outbound connections from Apache worker processes should receive similar scrutiny.

There are currently no vendor-published campaign-specific CVE-2026-119618 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or attacker infrastructure because Apache and the reviewed sources have not reported exploitation in the wild. This makes configuration assessment and behavior-based monitoring more valuable than static indicator matching.

CVE-2026-119618 Mitigation

The primary remediation is to upgrade affected Apache HTTP Server installations to version 2.4.71 or apply the corrected security package supplied by the operating system vendor. Apache 2.4.71 was released on November 11, 2026 and contains the upstream fix.

Organizations should prioritize internet-facing Apache deployments with HTTP/2 enabled because these systems expose the vulnerable functionality directly to untrusted network traffic.

Administrators should take the following steps:

  1. Inventory Apache HTTP Server deployments across production, development, cloud, and container environments.
  2. Identify installations running Apache 2.4.55 through 2.4.70.
  3. Verify whether mod_http2 is loaded.
  4. Inspect global and virtual-host Protocols directives for h2 or h2c.
  5. Upgrade upstream Apache deployments to 2.4.71 or later.
  6. Apply distribution-specific packages when Apache is managed through Debian, Red Hat, Amazon Linux, or another operating system vendor.
  7. Restart Apache after patching to ensure vulnerable worker processes are no longer running.
  8. Verify the effective HTTP server configuration after remediation.
  9. Review historical telemetry for suspicious activity on internet-facing systems that were exposed before patching.

Administrators should not assume that installing an operating system package with a version number below 2.4.71 means the system remains vulnerable. Vendors such as Red Hat backport security fixes into their own package versions, so the relevant distribution advisory should be treated as authoritative.

The official Apache advisory does not provide a workaround. However, organizations that cannot patch immediately can temporarily remove HTTP/2 from exposed configurations, eliminating access to the known vulnerable code path. Wiz recommends restricting the server to HTTP/1.1 until the update can be deployed.

For example:

Protocols http/1.1

Organizations applying this workaround should inspect all virtual hosts because a site-specific configuration can independently enable h2 or h2c.

Removing HTTP/2 can affect application performance and client behavior, so the change should be tested and treated as a temporary risk-reduction measure rather than a replacement for installing the security update.

The CVE-2026-119618 mitigation strategy should also include reducing unnecessary exposure. Administrative or internal Apache services that do not need direct internet connectivity should be restricted through network segmentation, load balancers, reverse proxies, firewall policies, or private addressing.

Organizations using standalone mod_h2 releases between 2.0.8 and 2.0.42 require particular attention. Apache identifies those releases as affected, while The Hacker News reported that no corrected standalone release had been published at the time of its November 12 report. Disabling HTTP/2 or migrating to an Apache HTTP Server package containing the upstream fix may therefore be necessary until an appropriate standalone update is available.

If suspicious activity is discovered, defenders should isolate the affected server where operationally feasible and preserve Apache access logs, error logs, system logs, process telemetry, network connections, and relevant memory or crash information.

Successful exploitation should be treated as potential server compromise rather than simply a service crash. Investigators should look for new files, webshells, altered application code, persistence mechanisms, stolen credentials, suspicious outbound traffic, and evidence of lateral movement.

Credentials accessible to the Apache process, including database passwords, API keys, cloud credentials, TLS private keys, or secrets stored in application configuration, should be reviewed and rotated when evidence suggests attacker-controlled code execution occurred.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-119618 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-119618 is a critical race condition in Apache HTTP Server’s mod_http2 module. Concurrent HTTP/2 processing can cause multiple threads to access shared memory without proper synchronization, resulting in heap corruption. A remote unauthenticated attacker who can reach an affected HTTP/2 service may be able to manipulate this corruption and execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the Apache server process.

When was CVE-2026-119618 first discovered?

Anthropic’s OSS Scanner reported the flaw to Apache on October 26, 2026. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research independently reported it on November 3. Apache publicly disclosed the vulnerability and released Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 containing the fix on November 11, 2026.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-119618 on systems?

Successful exploitation can corrupt Apache’s heap and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. An attacker may execute commands using the privileges of the Apache process, potentially access sensitive application data, modify files, establish persistence, disrupt services, or use the compromised server as an entry point for further attacks. Red Hat assigns the flaw a generic CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8.

Can CVE-2026-119618 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 remain vulnerable when mod_http2 and HTTP/2 are enabled unless the operating system vendor has backported the fix. As of November 12, 2026, the reviewed sources do not report confirmed exploitation in the wild, but reliable exploitation has been demonstrated in security research.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-119618?

Upgrade upstream Apache HTTP Server to 2.4.71 or later, or install the fixed package supplied by your Linux distribution. If immediate patching is impossible, temporarily disable HTTP/2 by removing h2 and h2c from the Protocols configuration and restrict unnecessary external access. Security teams should monitor Apache’s advisory and distribution security trackers for updated details for CVE-2026-119618 as additional exploit research and remediation information becomes available.

items.summary: .kadence-column488028_ad75a4-64 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column488028_ad75a4-64 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column488028_ad75a4-64 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column488028_ad75a4-64 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column488028_ad75a4-64 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column488028_ad75a4-64 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column488028_ad75a4-64{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column488028_ad75a4-64 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column488028_ad75a4-64 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article LEGO has taken BrickLink offline after detecting unusual activity The company has not confirmed a hack or whether customer data was affected Users should watch for suspicious payment requests and avoid reusing passwords LEGO collectors looking for a missing piece have a bigger problem to contend with: accessing the specialized marketplace BrickLink. LEGO has taken BrickLink offline after detecting what it calls “unusual activity.” The company says it is investigating before bringing the marketplace back, but has not disclosed whether attackers accessed its systems or whether customer information was affected. BrickLink allows users to buy and sell LEGO parts, sets, and minifigures, making it a useful resource for collectors and a business platform for independent sellers. LEGO acquired the fan-founded marketplace in 2019. Its disruption leaves more than unfinished builds on hold: sellers also depend on access to orders and their storefronts. The BrickLink website previously said it would remain unavailable until at least Wednesday, November 11. That date has now been removed, with no replacement given. We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform. Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink. Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues. This work is still on-going and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible. Updated: 11th November 2026 According to the BBC , LEGO had not provided details confirming a hack or explaining whether customer data was affected. Specialist LEGO publications reported that BrickLink went offline around November 5. An article published the following morning described a notice saying the site was unavailable while teams carried out “necessary work.” That report also noted that users could not access storefronts, profiles, order histories, or the Designer Program page. In November 2023, BrickLink also closed down after it noticed what turned out to be credential stuffing attacks. The BBC also reported the experience of a BrickLink customer who received repeated payment links for a limited-edition preorder she said she had already paid for. The dispute was subsequently resolved, and LEGO told the BBC it was not aware of wider payment issues. But there is no established connection between that payment problem and the activity that prompted the shutdown. How to stay safe Until we know what the issue is, it is hard to provide targeted advice, but users can take a few proportionate precautions: Watch for unexpected account or payment messages. A request to “restore access,” confirm payment information, or resolve an urgent account problem deserves scrutiny, because these are common phishing themes. Verify requests through an independent route. Use the official website or an established support channel rather than following links in an unexpected email or text. Use unique passwords. If your BrickLink password is also used elsewhere, change it on those other services now. Use a password manager to generate and store strong, unique passwords. Change your BrickLink password once the site is available again. BrickLink’s shutdown is disruptive, but the available evidence does not yet justify calling it a confirmed data breach. For now, the priority for users is to follow official updates, check unexpected payment requests carefully, and watch for scams exploiting the outage. Something feel off? Check it before you click. In this article
  • LEGO has taken BrickLink offline after detecting unusual activity
  • The company has not confirmed a hack or whether customer data was affected
  • Users should watch for suspicious payment requests and avoid reusing passwords

LEGO collectors looking for a missing piece have a bigger problem to contend with: accessing the specialized marketplace BrickLink.

LEGO has taken BrickLink offline after detecting what it calls “unusual activity.” The company says it is investigating before bringing the marketplace back, but has not disclosed whether attackers accessed its systems or whether customer information was affected.

BrickLink allows users to buy and sell LEGO parts, sets, and minifigures, making it a useful resource for collectors and a business platform for independent sellers. LEGO acquired the fan-founded marketplace in 2019. Its disruption leaves more than unfinished builds on hold: sellers also depend on access to orders and their storefronts.

The BrickLink website previously said it would remain unavailable until at least Wednesday, November 11. That date has now been removed, with no replacement given.

We took BrickLink offline after identifying unusual activity on the platform. Our immediate priority was to secure the site, protect our members and ensure the integrity of BrickLink.

Before bringing the site back online, we need to fully understand what has happened. That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues.

This work is still on-going and we appreciate your patience while we work to get things back online as soon as possible.

Updated: 11th November 2026

According to the BBC, LEGO had not provided details confirming a hack or explaining whether customer data was affected.

Specialist LEGO publications reported that BrickLink went offline around November 5. An article published the following morning described a notice saying the site was unavailable while teams carried out “necessary work.” That report also noted that users could not access storefronts, profiles, order histories, or the Designer Program page.

In November 2023, BrickLink also closed down after it noticed what turned out to be credential stuffing attacks.

The BBC also reported the experience of a BrickLink customer who received repeated payment links for a limited-edition preorder she said she had already paid for. The dispute was subsequently resolved, and LEGO told the BBC it was not aware of wider payment issues. But there is no established connection between that payment problem and the activity that prompted the shutdown.

How to stay safe

Until we know what the issue is, it is hard to provide targeted advice, but users can take a few proportionate precautions:

  • Watch for unexpected account or payment messages. A request to “restore access,” confirm payment information, or resolve an urgent account problem deserves scrutiny, because these are common phishing themes.
  • Verify requests through an independent route. Use the official website or an established support channel rather than following links in an unexpected email or text.
  • Use unique passwords. If your BrickLink password is also used elsewhere, change it on those other services now. Use a password manager to generate and store strong, unique passwords. Change your BrickLink password once the site is available again.

BrickLink’s shutdown is disruptive, but the available evidence does not yet justify calling it a confirmed data breach. For now, the priority for users is to follow official updates, check unexpected payment requests carefully, and watch for scams exploiting the outage.

items.title: nDiligence Releases Four-Year Study Identifying a Critical Supply-Chain Vulnerability Across 50 Platform Types
items.summary: San Francisco, California, USA, November 12th, 2026, CyberNewswire Four-year cybersecurity study finds all 50 types of software and devices examined vulnerable, with 46 rated Critical or High risk. nDiligence, Inc. today announced the release of Attack the Glass (ATG) research to the general public. The four-year study examines a cybersecurity vulnerability in how applications use people’s own devices to build what appears on screen, load data and run code while the application is in use. An attacker who exploits it can change what people see and what their software does, after every security check has passed. The research is free at https://atg.nDiligence.com . Much of the software people rely on, from web browsers and mobile apps to vehicle displays, medical devices and industrial control screens, builds its user interface on the device while it is running, a process called runtime client-side rendering. The code, data and media it assembles come from dozens or hundreds of suppliers: the organization’s own systems, its vendors and their vendors. An attacker who gains control of any one supplier gains placement and access inside the running application. Sign-in, encryption, Zero Trust, firewalls and code review all function before the code is loaded onto the device. Once loaded, the code is trusted, and nothing checks what it does. The attacker can change what appears on screen, capture what the person types and act with that person’s authority. In February 2024 the domain behind Polyfill.io, a code library loaded by more than 100,000 websites, was sold to a company the U.S. Treasury later sanctioned. The altered code ran for months on visitors’ devices, and no automated security tool detected it; researchers found it that June. The underlying vulnerability was never fixed. The ATG research documents how the same technique could deliver disinformation inside genuine news and election sites, show commanders and infrastructure operators a false picture, or hide safety alerts from selected users. Due to security concerns from this type of threat, the team behind nDiligence spent more than two years privately briefing governments before publishing. “People trust what they see with their own eyes. In the modern world we are constantly looking at screens, and we have grown to trust applications, websites, devices and companies, assuming they have 100% control over what is shown to us,” said Robert Beckett, Founder and CEO of nDiligence , who led the four-year research into the ATG vulnerability. “ATG demonstrates how an attacker can hijack that trust without detection or attribution. A commander, a grid operator, a voter or a reporter can be looking at a screen that every security system says is safe, and what it shows can be manipulated. Whoever controls the screen can influence what people believe, decide and do, with sophisticated targeting. And right now, nobody can tell when or where it is happening. The cybersecurity community needs to understand this vulnerability so we can protect the integrity of software systems across industries, governments and critical infrastructure.” Across the 10 categories examined, the research classifies five effects an attacker can achieve: deceive, disrupt, degrade, deny and destroy. All materials are free to share under Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) CLEAR, including a sixteen-chapter whitepaper, twenty online demonstrations and remediation playbooks. “ATG was discovered during our research into digital supply-chain threats,” said Beckett . “Our team has spent more than 15 years working in online threat intelligence and countering influence operations, which is why we recognized how the ATG vulnerability could be exploited. Since 2024, we have been working with researchers, vendors and governments to find ways to close this gap. Anyone who builds, operates or defends systems that people use to make critical decisions needs to understand and mitigate the ATG vulnerability.” About nDiligence nDiligence, Inc. is a supply-chain intelligence company that builds trusted provider networks and keeps the supply chains beneath them under continuous watch. Its founders bring decades of experience in internet supply chains and in national security and intelligence systems. The ATG research was self-funded. Learn more at https://www.ndiligence.com/ . Contact Chief Product Officer Anna Patterson nDiligence, Inc. press@ndiligence.com

items.title: CVE-2026-119618: What We Know About the Critical Apache mod_http2 Race Condition
items.summary: Critical Apache HTTP Server Vulnerability: What Defenders Need to Know On November 11, 2026, the Apache Software Foundation disclosed CVE-2026-119618 , a critical race condition in mod_http2, the module that provides HTTP/2 support in Apache HTTP Server. According to Apache’s advisory, the flaw can corrupt heap memory and may lead to remote code execution on the server. It affects Apache HTTP Server 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and standalone mod_h2 releases 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. Apache HTTP Server runs on a large share of internet-facing web servers and reverse proxies, so a critical bug in its HTTP/2 stack gets attention quickly. Public technical detail is still limited, though. This post covers what is known, what isn’t yet, and what we recommend defenders do now. The potential for unauthenticated remote code execution in a widely deployed web server makes this vulnerability a significant concern, particularly for internet-facing infrastructure. While public research has demonstrated exploitation, important questions remain about how reliably the vulnerability can be exploited across different configurations. Here’s what we know so far, what remains uncertain, and how defenders should prioritize their response. What the Vulnerability Is According to the official CVE-2026-119618 record , the vulnerability is a race condition in mod_http2’s assign_headers() function.The underlying issue involves improper synchronization between threads handling concurrent HTTP/2 requests. A worker thread can write to memory owned by another thread through a shared allocator, resulting in heap corruption that can potentially be leveraged for remote code execution. Because exploitation can occur remotely without authentication, vulnerable internet-facing systems present a particularly serious risk. Apache has fixed the vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 . Linux distributions and vendors that bundle httpd usually backport the fix under their own package versions, so the version string on a patched system may still read 2.4.x below 2.4.71. Check your vendor’s advisory rather than relying on the upstream version number alone. What We Know About Exploitability Apache’s initial advisory provides limited technical detail about exploitation requirements. However, Red Hat reports that public research has demonstrated reliable exploitation against a default-configured server with mod_http2 enabled. That distinction matters. While the vulnerability can lead to remote code execution, exploitability is not necessarily identical across every affected deployment. Exploit reliability. Reliable exploitation has been demonstrated against a default configuration, but consistency across different environments remains an important consideration. Configuration dependencies. Red Hat reports that memory allocation behavior influences exploitation complexity. In particular, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 use separate allocators for HTTP/2 streams, making exploitation substantially more difficult. Impact beyond a crash. Remote code execution has been demonstrated according to Red Hat’s assessment. The remaining challenge for defenders is identifying which exposed systems are susceptible to successful exploitation rather than relying on version-based detection alone. We are developing a working exploit internally to independently validate exploitability and better understand the conditions required for successful exploitation. Until those results are available, defenders should prioritize affected Apache deployments with HTTP/2 enabled, particularly those exposed to the internet. Identifying Exposed Systems An affected Apache version alone does not establish exploitability. The vulnerable HTTP/2 functionality must also be enabled. mod_http2 must be loaded. Check for LoadModule http2_module in your configuration, or run apachectl -M | grep http2. HTTP/2 must be enabled.
