Scheduling: More pods have been scheduled than spec.minMember , but the number of running pods hasn’t reached spec.minMember yet. Running: At least spec.minMember pods are running. Unknown: Some, but not all, of the required pods were scheduled. The rest can’t be scheduled (for example, due to insufficient resources), and the scheduler waits for controllers to recover them. Finished: The required pods completed successfully. Failed: At least one of the required pods has failed. You should expect a healthy gang to move from Pending or Scheduling to Running within the scheduling window you expect for that workload. If a gang remains Pending or Scheduling longer than expected, check the PodGroup events, associated pod events, and scheduler logs. A delay like this can indicate that the cluster cannot satisfy the gang’s resource requirements within the topology domain Kueue assigned, or that no available node satisfies scheduling requirements such as node selectors, taints, affinity, or resource availability. A gang stuck between Scheduling and Running with only partial placement may surface as Unknown rather than remaining in Scheduling . The Unknown phase differs from Failed , because the scheduler is still waiting on controllers to recover the unplaced pods, not reporting an outright failure. To distinguish an admission problem from a scheduler-level assembly problem, correlate PodGroup state with Kueue’s Workload status and admission metrics. If the Workload is still inadmissible, the issue is upstream of Coscheduling: Kueue has not admitted the job, so the fix is likely quota, priority, admission checks, or topology configuration. If the Workload is admitted and has a topology assignment, but the PodGroup remains Pending or Scheduling, the issue is later in the pipeline: Coscheduling and the kube-scheduler cannot assemble enough pods within the assigned placement and current cluster state. If a PodGroup reaches Failed , investigate the failed pods directly and look for common issues such as application failure, image or startup errors, or node disruption. Confirm scheduling effectiveness with training throughput signals Training frameworks are the software libraries that orchestrate distributed training, such as PyTorch , JAX , and Ray Train . Only by monitoring signals from these frameworks can you determine whether GPU cycles are producing completed training progress or being consumed by stalled communication. Ray is unique among these frameworks in its placement group model, which maps directly onto gang scheduling and gives it scheduling-aware observability. ray_placement_groups tracks the current number of placement groups by State, such as PENDING, CREATED, or REMOVED. A sustained increase in PENDING placement groups indicates that Ray is waiting for placement group resources to become available. ray_tasks tracks tasks by State, which can help show whether application work is accumulating while placement groups remain pending. When these signals rise together, Ray cannot satisfy its placement requirements. This can be a downstream effect of a Coscheduling assembly issue or a Kueue topology constraint problem rather than a simple application-layer slowdown. Other distributed training frameworks (including PyTorch DDP , Kubeflow operators, and Horovod ) don’t expose metrics that directly reflect the Kubernetes scheduler’s effectiveness. These frameworks do provide indirect indicators in the form of throughput metrics, such as steps per second, samples per second, and tokens per second. A throughput drop in these metrics alongside decreasing GPU interconnect bandwidth and PodGroup timeouts suggests a scheduling root cause. PodGroup timeouts confirm that gang assembly did not complete within the expected scheduling window. Correlating those timeouts with the Kueue Workload’s topology assignment and GPU, PCIe, and network telemetry data can help determine whether placement constraints contributed to the slowdown. Native Kubernetes scheduling: How v1.35 through v1.37 address AI training requirements Kueue and Coscheduling are out-of-tree components, installed and managed separately from Kubernetes. Kubernetes is beginning to add native scheduler capabilities that address the complex scheduling requirements this post describes, but those features are still early. Kubernetes v1.35 introduced native support for gang scheduling as an alpha feature. Kubernetes v1.36 added several related alpha features for AI training workloads, including topology-aware scheduling , workload-aware preemption, and initial Job controller integration via a feature gate. Kubernetes v1.36 also added a native PodGroup API , distinct from the out-of-tree PodGroup custom resource definition (CRD) used by the Coscheduling plugin. Kubernetes v1.37 graduated gang scheduling and workload-aware preemption to beta under the GenericWorkload feature gate, which remains disabled by default. The native TAS implementation enables the kube-scheduler to understand physical cluster topology and place pods within an appropriate topology domain, such as a rack or zone, without requiring Kueue to write node affinity rules into pod templates. These native capabilities are not yet a drop-in replacement for the Kueue and Coscheduling path described in this post. Gang scheduling and workload-aware preemption reached beta in v1.37 but ship disabled by default and still lack feature parity with Kueue and Coscheduling. Topology-aware workload scheduling remains alpha. Kueue and Coscheduling remain the production path for distributed training scheduling. Their monitoring signals, including admission queue depth, gang assembly state, topology placement, and GPU throughput, map directly to the concepts the native APIs expose. Teams that build observability into the current stack will have a working baseline when they evaluate or migrate to these native capabilities. Get started with gang scheduling and topology-aware placement Monitoring distributed AI training scheduling in Kubernetes requires visibility across components that standard tooling doesn’t naturally connect: Kueue’s admission queue, Coscheduling’s gang assembly, the GPU interconnect, and the training framework. Applying a common topology tag across all of these signals helps you monitor your clusters’ gang scheduling and TAS activity and ensure that your training jobs make efficient progress. To get started, read the Kueue documentation and the Coscheduling plugin documentation . This post originally appeared on the Datadog blog , where you can read the full version, including how to monitor and troubleshoot this stack in production.

items.title: Huntress uncovers SCKit: rogue ScreenConnect toolkit hits 288 hosts in 90 minutes
items.summary: Huntress researchers have detailed a fast-moving campaign in which attackers abused cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to install rogue clients and a custom toolkit, dubbed SCKit, on managed endpoints. At least 288 hosts across 48 Huntress-protected organisations were affected within around 90 minutes on 11 November, with roughly a third compromised in the first ten minutes. Rather than exploiting endpoints directly, the operator used ScreenConnect’s legitimate Run Command feature to execute commands as SYSTEM across many machines at once. Those commands silently installed an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client, followed by a dropper that fetched a decoder and an encrypted 16-file package of PowerShell, batch and config files. Each package was encrypted with keys tied to the individual machine’s ID. Hiding inside normal ScreenConnect traffic At the core of SCKit is a component Huntress calls RelayTrap. It takes over the legitimate client’s connection slot on the relay, so the machine still appears healthy to the managing technician. The toolkit also stops the genuine client and sets it to manual start, adds Microsoft Defender exclusions, creates AppLocker/SRP rules and a scheduled task named TrapWatch for persistence, and installs a second attacker-controlled client. Built to spread, not yet seen spreading The code contains logic intended to move from an infected endpoint to the technician who connects to it. In theory, it steals the technician’s .aspxauth session cookie, replays it against the panel, enumerates reachable sessions, and uploads a payload to the panel’s Shared Toolbox to run as SYSTEM elsewhere, deleting the toolbox item around 60 seconds later. Huntress stresses that this worm-like behaviour was largely reconstructed from code. The console-takeover attempt failed in every recovered host log it reviewed, and the firm has not confirmed a successful jump to a technician workstation or further endpoints. ConnectWise published an advisory on the evening of 11 November and, as a precaution, disabled five third-party extensions across more than 400 partner environments. At the time of the advisory, the initial access vector and full scope had not been identified. Affected builds named in the research are 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783. Isolate and clean affected hosts, removing the rogue client, the TrapWatch task, C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap\, SCKit files in %TEMP% and the RelayTrapLiteAlert Run key. End active ScreenConnect web sessions, rotate credentials, and revoke browser and identity-provider sessions. Use network IOCs from the report, but treat file hashes as weak indicators, as scripts are rebuilt per host. Those commands silently installed an attacker-controlled ScreenConnect client, followed by a dropper that fetched a decoder and an encrypted 16-file package of PowerShell, batch and config files. Each package was encrypted with keys tied to the individual machine’s ID.

The toolkit also stops the genuine client and sets it to manual start, adds Microsoft Defender exclusions, creates AppLocker/SRP rules and a scheduled task named TrapWatch for persistence, and installs a second attacker-controlled client.

The code contains logic intended to move from an infected endpoint to the technician who connects to it. In theory, it steals the technician’s .aspxauth session cookie, replays it against the panel, enumerates reachable sessions, and uploads a payload to the panel’s Shared Toolbox to run as SYSTEM elsewhere, deleting the toolbox item around 60 seconds later.

items.title: Cyber Agony Aunts Launch Christmas Campaign to Tackle Period Poverty
items.summary: The Cyber Agony Aunts , Amelia Hewitt and Rebecca Taylor, have launched Periods of Kindness, a Christmas campaign encouraging the cybersecurity community to come together to tackle period poverty across the UK. The initiative invites individuals and organisations to donate essential period products, which will be distributed to four charities and community organisations supporting people experiencing financial hardship and other challenges. Period poverty remains a significant issue in the UK. According to ActionAid’s 2026 UK poll, more than one in ten women and people who menstruate struggled to afford period products in the past year, with almost a quarter of those affected staying at home as a result. Some have been forced to use products for longer than is safe or rely on alternatives such as toilet paper or newspaper. Through Periods of Kindness, Hewitt and Taylor, who are authors and hosts of the ( 2026 Security Serious Unsung Heroes winning ) Cyber Agony Aunts podcast, hope to harness the generosity of the cybersecurity industry to make a difference beyond the sector. For Hewitt, who has spoken openly about her experiences with endometriosis, menstrual health is also a deeply personal issue. “Many of us can get through a working day without ever worrying whether we can afford period products. But for too many people, that simply isn’t the case. A period can mean missing school or work, making do with something unsafe, or choosing between products and food. No one should have to live like that,” said Hewitt. “Periods of Kindness is our way of turning that awareness into action, so more people can get on with their lives with dignity.” Taylor added: “I feel passionately that no one deserves to experience period poverty. I want us to bring the same care we have for people in our cyber community to those beyond it, too. You don’t have to work in cyber to join us: if you can donate or share the appeal, you can be part of something incredible this Christmas.” Supporting Four Organisations Donations collected through the campaign will benefit four organisations working to support vulnerable and disadvantaged communities. RBKares – Royal Borough of Kingston Cares : A volunteer-run charity providing practical assistance to people in need, including those experiencing homelessness, refugees and care home residents. Alana House : A Reading-based women’s community project run by Parents And Children Together (PACT), offering confidential support to women facing multiple disadvantages and complex needs. Reading College : Part of Activate Learning, the college will receive essential period products to support disadvantaged students. Freedom4girls : A charity tackling period poverty through product donations, menstrual health education and awareness campaigns, with initiatives in the UK, Kenya and Uganda. How the Cybersecurity Community Can Get Involved Supporters can contribute to the campaign by purchasing period products through a dedicated Amazon wishlist until 31 December 2026 . Those unable to donate are encouraged to share the appeal with colleagues, friends and their wider networks. The donated products will be packed for distribution on 22 January 2027, during an event hosted by UK managed cybersecurity provider Custodian360. Nikki Webb, Director at Custodian360, commented: “We’re so happy to support Periods of Kindness and to host the packing day for this thoughtful campaign. No one should have to go without essential period products, and we’re delighted to stand alongside Amelia, Rebecca and the wider cyber community to help. It’s a chance to come together, give back and show what kindness can look like in action.” The campaign is open to everyone, whether they work in cybersecurity or simply want to contribute to the cause. To support Periods of Kindness, visit the campaign’s Amazon wishlist before 31 December 2026.

items.title: Why scammers want you to allow push notifications
items.summary: A website asks you to click “Allow” to start a quiz or read an interesting story. A little later, your device starts warning you about viruses, missed payments, or legal trouble. While every message may look like a new security problem, the cause could be a permission you granted earlier. For scammers, browser push notifications turn a passing visit into something much more valuable: access to your attention after you have left their website. Two investigations—including our own research into deceptive quiz sites and HUMAN Security’s investigation of an operation called Pushpaganda —show how that permission can become a tool for repeated advertising, scareware, and fraud. Ordinarily, a deceptive website has a limited opportunity to influence you. Once you leave, its sales pitch disappears. A simple browser push notification permission changes that relationship. A website you’ve authorized can send browser notifications even when you’re not visiting it. Depending on the platform and browser configuration, those messages can appear even when the browser is not visibly open. Just what scammers need That gives scammers several advantages: Repeat opportunities to get a click. Instead of relying on one visit, they can send more messages to bring you back to their sites. A more convincing place to display a lie. Notifications appear through the browser and operating system, while their wording and imagery can impersonate security alerts, financial messages, or people you know. Distance from the original trick. By the time alarming messages start appearing, you may not remember which website received permission, let alone connect the alerts to an innocent-looking quiz. More chances to make money. The resulting traffic can feed advertising, affiliate promotions, scams, and unwanted downloads. Allowing notifications doesn’t install malware . But scammers can use them to trick you into clicking a harmful link or downloading something dangerous. That explains why your device can display frightening warnings while a malware scan finds nothing wrong. The campaigns The quiz that came with an unwanted extra Our investigation, published on March 9, began with customers who thought their devices were infected. Malwarebytes scans came up clean. Screenshots helped our Malware Removal Support team identify the real source of the trouble: web push notifications. While the quizzes were real, the trick was making people think they had to allow the notifications to take them. Clicking “Start the quiz” first brought up the browser’s notification permission request. Behind that legitimate browser prompt, the website displayed its own instruction: “Click ‘Allow’ to continue.” The page made it seem you had to allow the notifications to take the quiz, when it actually meant agreeing to receive future messages. From clickbait to a notification loop On April 14, HUMAN Security’s Satori researchers published a larger example of the same underlying strategy. They called it Pushpaganda . Instead of quizzes, the operation used sensational articles and images, many showing signs of AI generation. Headlines promised attention-grabbing financial developments or implausible technology bargains. The content appeared in Google Discover feeds, exposing it to Android and Chrome users. Researchers could not establish whether those placements resulted from paid promotion or search optimization. Once someone visited an associated website, the operation prompted them to enable notifications. The messages that followed had little to do with the article that attracted the visitor. Researchers observed fake arrest warrants, false financial alerts, and notifications mimicking missed calls from “Mom” or other family members. Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows. TRY IT NOW Scam Guard stats The graph shows weekly counts of reports classified by Scam Guard as matching quiz-site notification abuse (red) and Pushpaganda (blue), based on the information provided by users. The counts show reports over time linked to these campaigns. They don’t represent unique victims, confirmed infections, or total campaign activity. For context: HUMAN Security’s Satori researchers observed roughly 240 million advertising bid requests associated with Pushpaganda domains in a single seven-day period at the operation’s peak. A bid request asks advertisers in real-time to bid for an opportunity to show an ad. In a push notification ad auction, the winning ad is sent as a notification to someone who has allowed them. Note the dip after the reports came out. It takes time to rebuild the infrastructure, but criminals will do so if they think it’s worth the investment. How to stay safe Allow notifications only when you want ongoing messages from a site. A few guidelines that may help you: Don’t click on prompts until you’re sure what they will set in motion. Treat “Allow notifications to continue” as a red flag, particularly on quizzes, video pages, or unfamiliar websites. Use web protection. Malwarebytes Browser Guard is a free tool that can help block malicious websites. If you’re haunted by unwanted alerts, they might be web push notifications. Here’s how to identify the website sending them and turn them off in several popular browsers . On supported Android devices, Chrome notifications include an Unsubscribe option. Use that built-in control rather than a link inside a suspicious message. When you receive an unwanted website notification through Chrome on Android: Swipe down from the top of the screen to open Android’s notification shade. Look for an Unsubscribe action on the notification. If it is present, tap it to stop future notifications from that website. Chrome also provides Undo if you unsubscribe accidentally. If Unsubscribe is not present, open Chrome and go to More > Settings > Site settings > Notifications . Review the allowed websites and block the offending site. You don’t need to follow a link in the suspicious notification to manage its permission. “One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” According to CNET. Read their review →

“Click ‘Allow’ to continue.”

Researchers observed fake arrest warrants, false financial alerts, and notifications mimicking missed calls from “Mom” or other family members.

Scam or legit? Scam Guard knows.

items.title: Bring Your Own CA: Palo Alto Networks Joins the Imperva SSL Integration Center
items.summary: In August we introduced the Imperva SSL Integration Center with one idea behind it: the certificates protecting your applications should be governed where you already govern certificates, and deploy to Imperva Cloud WAF without anyone copying a key. DigiCert Trust Lifecycle Manager was the first integration. Keyfactor Command followed. Today the Integration Center adds the platform that a large share of enterprise PKI teams run machine identity management on: Venafi, now part of Palo Alto Networks, delivered as CyberArk Certificate Manager and Palo Alto Networks Next-Gen Trust Security. The timing is not an accident. Under the CA/Browser Forum timeline, maximum public TLS certificate lifetimes drop to 200 days from March 2026, 100 days from March 2027 and 47 days from March 2029. Every manual step in a renewal becomes a step you repeat eight times a year, and the manual step breaks first. A WAF that sits outside the automation is the step most likely to break. What ships: Imperva WAF as a machine In Certificate Manager terms, an application that receives certificates is a machine. The platform discovers what is installed on it, provisions certificates to it and records every installation. Imperva Cloud WAF is now a machine type, listed alongside the load balancers, gateways and firewalls the platform already manages, in both of the platform’s current homes: CyberArk Certificate Manager – SaaS , the SaaS platform formerly known as Venafi as a Service, where the Imperva WAF machine sits in the Installations section alongside other targets. Palo Alto Networks Next-Gen Trust Security , the same capability under the Palo Alto Networks name, with the Imperva pages updated on 4 November 2026. In the platform’s own words, creating the machine lets it “discover the certificates of the sites in your Imperva Cloud Web Application Firewall (WAF) account and provision custom certificates to them.” With the cloud connector, there is no automation host to stand up and no script to maintain: the platform talks to the Imperva API, authenticated by an API ID and key from your Imperva account, and the credentials can be drawn from a credential manager integration rather than typed into a form. Teams whose policy keeps such connections inside their own network can run the same connector on a VSatellite instead. For WAF Gateway, the self-hosted platform (CyberArk Trust Protection Foundation, formerly Venafi Trust Protection Platform) carries a separate, long-standing Imperva MX driver that provisions key pairs to the Imperva management server for on-premises deployments. That path has its own prerequisites and limits; the documentation lists them. How it works: provisioning certificates to Imperva Cloud WAF The whole setup is two screens in the certificate platform and one API key in the Imperva Cloud Security Console. Generate an API key in Imperva under Account > Account Management > API Keys, with the entitlement to manage custom certificates for the sites you will provision to, and copy the API ID and API Key. Note the numeric Site ID of each target site from its General settings. Create the machine. Choose Imperva WAF as the machine type (or Imperva WAF (VSatellite) to run the connector in your network), confirm the hostname (the default is my.imperva.com) and port 443, supply admin credentials directly or select stored credentials from a credential manager integration, enter the API ID and API Key, and click Test Access. Continue is enabled only when the connection test succeeds. Set the discovery and provisioning schedule for the machine, the same way as for any other machine on the platform. Provision. From Insights > Certificate Installations > Machines, select Provision on the Imperva WAF row, choose the certificate from the inventory, check its subject, validity and fingerprint, enter the Site ID, and save. Push upon saving is on by default; turn it off to stage the certificate without deploying it. The platform provisions the certificate to the Imperva site and writes an installation record on the Installations tab, so the WAF now shows up in the same inventory, the same reports and the same renewal workflow as everything else the platform manages. The target site must already exist in Imperva with a site ID; the integration installs to it, it does not create it. What this means for your team One system of record, now including the WAF. Certificates governed in Certificate Manager deploy to Imperva sites on the platform’s schedule, with the installation recorded where your auditors already look. The WAF stops being the exception to your automation. Nothing to host by default. The connection runs from the platform to the Imperva API. No automation server, no post-enrollment script, no credentials pasted into a job definition: stored credentials can come from a credential manager integration. Your certificate is the one served. Since the 14 September release, when a site holds a valid custom certificate and a valid Imperva site certificate for the same host, Cloud WAF serves yours; the Imperva certificate is the fallback only if yours is invalid or does not cover the host. Bring-your-own-CA means exactly that. Ready for the 47-day clock. Shorter lifetimes are a scheduling problem, and the platform already carries a 47-Day Validity Readiness Dashboard. With the WAF inside the loop, the renewal that used to need a person now needs a schedule. No change of CA. You keep your issuing CAs, your policies and your approval workflows; the WAF is one more place they deploy to. Both estates covered. Cloud WAF through the SaaS platform, WAF Gateway through the self-hosted driver, so a hybrid estate does not need two processes. Imperva-managed certificates: nothing changes Many Cloud WAF customers let Imperva issue and renew their certificates, and for them nothing changes: Imperva site certificates keep renewing on their own, with no action and no integration to configure. The Integration Center is for the teams that run their own CA and PKI processes and want the WAF to follow them. Nobody is being asked to switch certificate authorities in either direction. A wider Integration Center Each certificate lifecycle platform reaches the Integration Center in its own shape: DigiCert through a post-enrollment agent script, Keyfactor through a Universal Orchestrator extension, and now Venafi through the machine model of CyberArk Certificate Manager and Palo Alto Networks Next-Gen Trust Security. The destination is the same Imperva API every time, which is why the customer-side work stays at one API key and one site ID whichever platform you run. Further platforms are in progress. The partnership also reaches past the WAF. Palo Alto Networks is a Thales technology partner across the wider portfolio, and the same certificate platform that now feeds Imperva can draw on Thales Luna HSMs for key protection where the policy demands it. Get started with Imperva WAF in Next-Gen Trust Security If you run CyberArk Certificate Manager or Palo Alto Networks Next-Gen Trust Security today, the integration is already in your Installations menu and there is nothing to install. Three steps get you to the first certificate the platform provisions: In the Imperva Cloud Security Console, create an API key under Account > Account Management > API Keys with the entitlement to manage custom certificates, and note the Site ID of each site the platform will serve. In the certificate platform, follow Create an Imperva WAF Machine , then Provision to an Imperva WAF . The same steps under the CyberArk name are in the Imperva WAF machine documentation. Running WAF Gateway? Start from the Imperva MX driver documentation for Trust Protection Foundation and check the version prerequisites against your deployment. The Imperva side of the setup, including API key permissions and the custom certificate priority rules, is in the SSL Integration Center documentation . If 47-day renewals are still a plan rather than a process in your organization, five steps to prepare is the place to start. The certificate manager that already knows every certificate you own now knows the one on your WAF as well: who requested it, which CA issued it, when it renews, and that the platform installed it on schedule. When the 47-day clock starts in March 2029, the WAF renewal is already one more scheduled job, recorded where the rest of them are.

In August we introduced the Imperva SSL Integration Center with one idea behind it: the certificates protecting your applications should be governed where you already govern certificates, and deploy to Imperva Cloud WAF without anyone copying a key. DigiCert Trust Lifecycle Manager was the first integration. Keyfactor Command followed. Today the Integration Center adds the platform that a large share of enterprise PKI teams run machine identity management on: Venafi, now part of Palo Alto Networks, delivered as CyberArk Certificate Manager and Palo Alto Networks Next-Gen Trust Security.

The timing is not an accident. Under the CA/Browser Forum timeline, maximum public TLS certificate lifetimes drop to 200 days from March 2026, 100 days from March 2027 and 47 days from March 2029. Every manual step in a renewal becomes a step you repeat eight times a year, and the manual step breaks first. A WAF that sits outside the automation is the step most likely to break.

What ships: Imperva WAF as a machine

In Certificate Manager terms, an application that receives certificates is a machine. The platform discovers what is installed on it, provisions certificates to it and records every installation. Imperva Cloud WAF is now a machine type, listed alongside the load balancers, gateways and firewalls the platform already manages, in both of the platform’s current homes:

  • CyberArk Certificate Manager – SaaS, the SaaS platform formerly known as Venafi as a Service, where the Imperva WAF machine sits in the Installations section alongside other targets.
  • Palo Alto Networks Next-Gen Trust Security, the same capability under the Palo Alto Networks name, with the Imperva pages updated on 4 November 2026.

In the platform’s own words, creating the machine lets it “discover the certificates of the sites in your Imperva Cloud Web Application Firewall (WAF) account and provision custom certificates to them.” With the cloud connector, there is no automation host to stand up and no script to maintain: the platform talks to the Imperva API, authenticated by an API ID and key from your Imperva account, and the credentials can be drawn from a credential manager integration rather than typed into a form. Teams whose policy keeps such connections inside their own network can run the same connector on a VSatellite instead.

For WAF Gateway, the self-hosted platform (CyberArk Trust Protection Foundation, formerly Venafi Trust Protection Platform) carries a separate, long-standing Imperva MX driver that provisions key pairs to the Imperva management server for on-premises deployments. That path has its own prerequisites and limits; the documentation lists them.

How it works: provisioning certificates to Imperva Cloud WAF

The whole setup is two screens in the certificate platform and one API key in the Imperva Cloud Security Console.

  1. Generate an API key in Imperva under Account > Account Management > API Keys, with the entitlement to manage custom certificates for the sites you will provision to, and copy the API ID and API Key. Note the numeric Site ID of each target site from its General settings.
  2. Create the machine. Choose Imperva WAF as the machine type (or Imperva WAF (VSatellite) to run the connector in your network), confirm the hostname (the default is my.imperva.com) and port 443, supply admin credentials directly or select stored credentials from a credential manager integration, enter the API ID and API Key, and click Test Access. Continue is enabled only when the connection test succeeds.
  3. Set the discovery and provisioning schedule for the machine, the same way as for any other machine on the platform.
  4. Provision. From Insights > Certificate Installations > Machines, select Provision on the Imperva WAF row, choose the certificate from the inventory, check its subject, validity and fingerprint, enter the Site ID, and save. Push upon saving is on by default; turn it off to stage the certificate without deploying it.

The platform provisions the certificate to the Imperva site and writes an installation record on the Installations tab, so the WAF now shows up in the same inventory, the same reports and the same renewal workflow as everything else the platform manages. The target site must already exist in Imperva with a site ID; the integration installs to it, it does not create it.

What this means for your team
  • One system of record, now including the WAF. Certificates governed in Certificate Manager deploy to Imperva sites on the platform’s schedule, with the installation recorded where your auditors already look. The WAF stops being the exception to your automation.
  • Nothing to host by default. The connection runs from the platform to the Imperva API. No automation server, no post-enrollment script, no credentials pasted into a job definition: stored credentials can come from a credential manager integration.
  • Your certificate is the one served. Since the 14 September release, when a site holds a valid custom certificate and a valid Imperva site certificate for the same host, Cloud WAF serves yours; the Imperva certificate is the fallback only if yours is invalid or does not cover the host. Bring-your-own-CA means exactly that.
  • Ready for the 47-day clock. Shorter lifetimes are a scheduling problem, and the platform already carries a 47-Day Validity Readiness Dashboard. With the WAF inside the loop, the renewal that used to need a person now needs a schedule.
  • No change of CA. You keep your issuing CAs, your policies and your approval workflows; the WAF is one more place they deploy to.
  • Both estates covered. Cloud WAF through the SaaS platform, WAF Gateway through the self-hosted driver, so a hybrid estate does not need two processes.
Imperva-managed certificates: nothing changes

Many Cloud WAF customers let Imperva issue and renew their certificates, and for them nothing changes: Imperva site certificates keep renewing on their own, with no action and no integration to configure. The Integration Center is for the teams that run their own CA and PKI processes and want the WAF to follow them. Nobody is being asked to switch certificate authorities in either direction.

A wider Integration Center

Each certificate lifecycle platform reaches the Integration Center in its own shape: DigiCert through a post-enrollment agent script, Keyfactor through a Universal Orchestrator extension, and now Venafi through the machine model of CyberArk Certificate Manager and Palo Alto Networks Next-Gen Trust Security. The destination is the same Imperva API every time, which is why the customer-side work stays at one API key and one site ID whichever platform you run. Further platforms are in progress.

The partnership also reaches past the WAF. Palo Alto Networks is a Thales technology partner across the wider portfolio, and the same certificate platform that now feeds Imperva can draw on Thales Luna HSMs for key protection where the policy demands it.

Get started with Imperva WAF in Next-Gen Trust Security

If you run CyberArk Certificate Manager or Palo Alto Networks Next-Gen Trust Security today, the integration is already in your Installations menu and there is nothing to install. Three steps get you to the first certificate the platform provisions:

  1. In the Imperva Cloud Security Console, create an API key under Account > Account Management > API Keys with the entitlement to manage custom certificates, and note the Site ID of each site the platform will serve.
  2. In the certificate platform, follow Create an Imperva WAF Machine, then Provision to an Imperva WAF. The same steps under the CyberArk name are in the Imperva WAF machine documentation.
  3. Running WAF Gateway? Start from the Imperva MX driver documentation for Trust Protection Foundation and check the version prerequisites against your deployment.

The Imperva side of the setup, including API key permissions and the custom certificate priority rules, is in the SSL Integration Center documentation. If 47-day renewals are still a plan rather than a process in your organization, five steps to prepare is the place to start.

The certificate manager that already knows every certificate you own now knows the one on your WAF as well: who requested it, which CA issued it, when it renews, and that the platform installed it on schedule. When the 47-day clock starts in March 2029, the WAF renewal is already one more scheduled job, recorded where the rest of them are.

The post Bring Your Own CA: Palo Alto Networks Joins the Imperva SSL Integration Center appeared first on Blog.

items.title: PHP2Shell and Node2Shell: Find, Fix, and Verify Across Your Web Apps and APIs
items.summary: Key Takeaways Neither flaw is in your application code. Every app and API on a vulnerable runtime inherits the risk. PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) is fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Both are on the CISA KEV list. PHP2Shell was added on October 26. Node2Shell followed on October 27. Qualys TotalAppSec tests the application and the APIs with four non-intrusive QIDs for detection of vulnerabilities and two intrusive QIDs for verification of the fix. Patching fixes the runtime. A rescan confirms the fix worked and the application is no longer exposed. On October 21, fixes came out for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two critical flaws in the runtimes beneath your web apps and APIs. Five days later, PHP2Shell was on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list , and Node2Shell followed the next day. Attackers had been probing PHP2Shell four days before a patch even existed . With a timeline that short, the standard response of finding hosts, upgrading, and closing the ticket is not enough. Patched is a claim about a server. However, attackers really connect to the applications and APIs running on them. The question for application security teams is not whether PHP and Node.js were upgraded. It is whether an attacker can still reach the flaw through any application you run, and how you would know. This post covers how the two flaws impact your application estate, where most response plans break, and how Qualys TotalAppSec turns a runtime flaw into a finding you can fix and verify. A Runtime Flaw Is an Application Risk You Inherit Neither flaw is in your application code, which is why code scans, reviews and tests won’t flag them. Every application and API running on a vulnerable runtime inherits the exposure. PHP2Shell is a wide-scale problem. Qualys Threat Research Unit analyzed anonymized data from more than 10,000 customers and found 167 million PHP installations . Of the 156 million where the PHP version could be identified, 73% are on internet-facing assets. About 71% of the same 156 million run end-of-life or end-of-support versions that will likely never get a vendor patch, and only 199,000 were patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure . Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js) hides in plain sight. Apps can be exposed even if they never call a Brotli API , because frameworks or dependencies may decompress attacker-controlled data. Node.js fetch() and Express 5 request-body parsing are examples of such attack vectors. As with PHP, end-of-life Node.js lines, including 25.x, 23.x and 20.x, get no fix and must move to a supported release. In practice, the exposed estate includes customer portals, CMS-powered sites, microservices and the APIs that connect them. It also includes anything that fetches or accepts compressed content. Attackers are not waiting for your patch cycle Details of PHP2Shell leaked before the coordinated release . Amazon Threat Intelligence spotted attackers targeting it four days before patches shipped , though early activity was mostly scanning, fingerprinting and non-working exploits. Then it escalated. CISA added PHP2Shell to its catalog on October 26 and Node2Shell on October 27 . Confirmed code execution: a researcher’s honeypots recorded confirmed remote code execution with usable memory disclosure against Apache mod_php running PHP 8.4.26. Scale of attacks: Delft University’s Threat Intelligence Lab tracked more than 50,000 PHP2Shell exploitation requests from over 600 IP addresses across 70 countries. Node2Shell: P ublic exploit code is available, and exploitation attempts have been observed in the wild. What’s at stake: R esearchers have shown that PHP worker memory can be disclosed without authentication, exposing passwords, authentication tokens and API keys. To be precise: CISA hasn’t said which organizations were compromised, and the confirmed PHP exploit was on a deliberately favorable single-worker setup. The safe reading is that attackers have working exploits and are scanning widely, so treat any unpatched internet-facing app as a target. Find, fix and verify PHP2Shell and Node2Shell across your apps and APIs with TotalAppSec . Where Most Response Plans Break Most plans follow the same path: inventory hosts, upgrade, restart, close the ticket. That works until one of three gaps appears. In each case, the fix was applied in one place, but the attacker reaches the application through another. The application nobody owns You can’t test or patch what isn’t in your inventory. Forgotten microsites, acquired apps, and shadow APIs can run old runtimes, and they are the ones nobody is watching. A version string is a hint, not proof Proxies can strip the headers that reveal a PHP version, so a version-based check can miss a vulnerable app. Distribution builds can carry a backported fix under an older version number, so the same check can flag a fixed one. Neither a version banner nor a package list tells you how the application behaves when an attacker sends a request. Patched on disk is not patched in production Running processes keep the vulnerable code in memory until services such as PHP-FPM or long-running Node.js apps restart. Servers can also carry more than one PHP copy, so upgrading one leaves another. The fix only counts if the patched runtime is the one serving requests. A response built to end in proof An industry-neutral response has five steps, and the fourth is the one most teams skip. Find every runtime and application. Inventory the web apps and APIs behind your internet-facing services and the runtimes under them. Include end-of-life versions, containers, vendor-bundled runtimes and apps nobody owns. Scan, then rank by exposure. Start with internet-facing apps. Most teams can’t tell which apps use Apache mod_php or decompress untrusted Brotli data until they scan, so test first and rank the confirmed findings. Fix, then restart. Upgrade to a fixed version or your distribution’s backported build, and restart every service that loads the runtime. If you can’t patch yet, apply the vendor’s interim mitigations and restrict access to the service. Prove it from the outside. Retest the same applications and APIs, and treat any remaining finding as an incomplete fix. Also check for signs of compromise from before the patch, since exploitation began early. Make it repeatable. The next trending CVE will start the same race. A standing process beats a scramble. How to detect PHP2Shell and Node2Shell in web apps and APIs with TotalAppSec Qualys TotalAppSec brings AI-powered, unified risk management to web apps and APIs. For PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, it tests the application itself over HTTP, the same path an attacker uses, not just the host. Six new QIDs cover both web applications and APIs. Two kinds of evidence: Potential findings (QIDs 520310 and 520404) read PHP version signals from response headers and application cookies. Confirmed findings (QIDs 533086 and 533203) observe behavior in the live application: how PHP handles a session ID with an invalid character, and how Node.js handles a crafted Brotli payload. Four of the six checks are non-intrusive and can be safely used in production. A safe way to verify: The two intrusive checks (QIDs 533068 and 533085) stress the application and can crash an unpatched one. A ready starting point for the next one: TotalAppSec includes two system-generated option profiles for scanning trending CVEs such as PHP2Shell and Node2Shell. To run a PHP2Shell and Node2Shell web application scan, choose a profile, select your apps by name or tag, and launch. The product tour below walks you through each step. Your scheduled scans may already include the four non-intrusive QIDs, because they are part of the Core, OWASP Top 10 and Everything option profiles and of AI-powered scans. Each finding attaches to a named application or API, so its owner can act on it. After the fix and restart, rescan the same applications. If a QID still reports, the patched runtime isn’t the one serving those requests. TotalAppSec shows what is exposed at the application and API layer. The runtime underneath lives on hosts, in images and in cloud workloads, where Qualys VMDR, TotalCloud and Container Security find vulnerable PHP and Node.js components. The pattern will repeat. The next critical runtime flaw may also sit outside your own code, and attackers will again move faster than most patch cycles. The teams that cope best aren’t the ones scrambling hardest in the first week. They already know which web apps and APIs they have, can see which are exposed, and can confirm a fix actually worked. Patched is a claim about a server. Proof is a finding about an application. Qualys TotalAppSec gives you that application-level view, with ready-made trending vulnerability profiles to start from. Get Our Free Services Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) Which option profiles include the PHP2Shell and Node2Shell QIDs? The four non-intrusive QIDs (520310, 533086, 520404 and 533203) are in the Trending Vulnerability Options profile, and also in the Core, OWASP Top 10 and Everything option profiles. The two intrusive QIDs (533068 and 533085) are only in Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options. Does an AI-powered scan test for the new QIDs? Yes, for the four non-intrusive QIDs. The two intrusive QIDs are not part of AI-powered scans, so run them separately with the Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options profile. When can a scan miss PHP2Shell or Node2Shell? Upgrade the runtime, restart the affected services, then rescan the same applications with Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options on patched systems or outside production, with approvals and a maintenance window. If a QID is still reported, the fix is incomplete, so check that the patched runtime is serving requests.

Key Takeaways
  • Neither flaw is in your application code. Every app and API on a vulnerable runtime inherits the risk. 
  • PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) is fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. 
  • Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. 
  • Both are on the CISA KEV list. PHP2Shell was added on October 26. Node2Shell followed on October 27. 
  • Qualys TotalAppSec tests the application and the APIs with four non-intrusive QIDs for detection of vulnerabilities and two intrusive QIDs for verification of the fix.  
  • Patching fixes the runtime. A rescan confirms the fix worked and the application is no longer exposed. 

On October 21, fixes came out for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two critical flaws in the runtimes beneath your web apps and APIs. Five days later, PHP2Shell was on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list, and Node2Shell followed the next day. Attackers had been probing PHP2Shell four days before a patch even existed. 

With a timeline that short, the standard response of finding hosts, upgrading, and closing the ticket is not enough. Patched is a claim about a server. However, attackers really connect to the applications and APIs running on them. The question for application security teams is not whether PHP and Node.js were upgraded. It is whether an attacker can still reach the flaw through any application you run, and how you would know. 

This post covers how the two flaws impact your application estate, where most response plans break, and how Qualys TotalAppSec turns a runtime flaw into a finding you can fix and verify. 

A Runtime Flaw Is an Application Risk You Inherit 

Neither flaw is in your application code, which is why code scans, reviews and tests won’t flag them. Every application and API running on a vulnerable runtime inherits the exposure. 

PHP2Shell is a wide-scale problem. Qualys Threat Research Unit analyzed anonymized data from more than 10,000 customers and found 167 million PHP installations. Of the 156 million where the PHP version could be identified, 73% are on internet-facing assets. About 71% of the same 156 million run end-of-life or end-of-support versions that will likely never get a vendor patch, and only 199,000 were patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure.  

Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js) hides in plain sight. Apps can be exposed even if they never call a Brotli API, because frameworks or dependencies may decompress attacker-controlled data. Node.js fetch() and Express 5 request-body parsing are examples of such attack vectors. As with PHP, end-of-life Node.js lines, including 25.x, 23.x and 20.x, get no fix and must move to a supported release. 

In practice, the exposed estate includes customer portals, CMS-powered sites, microservices and the APIs that connect them. It also includes anything that fetches or accepts compressed content. 

Attackers are not waiting for your patch cycle 

Details of PHP2Shell leaked before the coordinated release. Amazon Threat Intelligence spotted attackers targeting it four days before patches shipped, though early activity was mostly scanning, fingerprinting and non-working exploits. Then it escalated. CISA added PHP2Shell to its catalog on October 26 and Node2Shell on October 27. 

  • Confirmed code execution: a researcher’s honeypots recorded confirmed remote code execution with usable memory disclosure against Apache mod_php running PHP 8.4.26. 
  • Scale of attacks: Delft University’s Threat Intelligence Lab tracked more than 50,000 PHP2Shell exploitation requests from over 600 IP addresses across 70 countries. 
  • Node2Shell: Public exploit code is available, and exploitation attempts have been observed in the wild. 
  • What’s at stake: Researchers have shown that PHP worker memory can be disclosed without authentication, exposing passwords, authentication tokens and API keys. 

To be precise: CISA hasn’t said which organizations were compromised, and the confirmed PHP exploit was on a deliberately favorable single-worker setup. The safe reading is that attackers have working exploits and are scanning widely, so treat any unpatched internet-facing app as a target. 

Find, fix and verify PHP2Shell and Node2Shell across your apps and APIs with TotalAppSec. 

Where Most Response Plans Break 

Most plans follow the same path: inventory hosts, upgrade, restart, close the ticket. That works until one of three gaps appears. In each case, the fix was applied in one place, but the attacker reaches the application through another. 

The application nobody owns 

You can’t test or patch what isn’t in your inventory. Forgotten microsites, acquired apps, and shadow APIs can run old runtimes, and they are the ones nobody is watching. 

A version string is a hint, not proof 

Proxies can strip the headers that reveal a PHP version, so a version-based check can miss a vulnerable app. Distribution builds can carry a backported fix under an older version number, so the same check can flag a fixed one. Neither a version banner nor a package list tells you how the application behaves when an attacker sends a request. 

Patched on disk is not patched in production 

Running processes keep the vulnerable code in memory until services such as PHP-FPM or long-running Node.js apps restart. Servers can also carry more than one PHP copy, so upgrading one leaves another. The fix only counts if the patched runtime is the one serving requests. 

A response built to end in proof 

An industry-neutral response has five steps, and the fourth is the one most teams skip. 

  1. Find every runtime and application. Inventory the web apps and APIs behind your internet-facing services and the runtimes under them. Include end-of-life versions, containers, vendor-bundled runtimes and apps nobody owns. 
  1. Scan, then rank by exposure. Start with internet-facing apps. Most teams can’t tell which apps use Apache mod_php or decompress untrusted Brotli data until they scan, so test first and rank the confirmed findings. 
  1. Fix, then restart. Upgrade to a fixed version or your distribution’s backported build, and restart every service that loads the runtime. If you can’t patch yet, apply the vendor’s interim mitigations and restrict access to the service. 
  1. Prove it from the outside. Retest the same applications and APIs, and treat any remaining finding as an incomplete fix. Also check for signs of compromise from before the patch, since exploitation began early. 
  1. Make it repeatable. The next trending CVE will start the same race. A standing process beats a scramble. 
How to detect PHP2Shell and Node2Shell in web apps and APIs with TotalAppSec 

Qualys TotalAppSec brings AI-powered, unified risk management to web apps and APIs. For PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, it tests the application itself over HTTP, the same path an attacker uses, not just the host. Six new QIDs cover both web applications and APIs. 

Two kinds of evidence: Potential findings (QIDs 520310 and 520404) read PHP version signals from response headers and application cookies. Confirmed findings (QIDs 533086 and 533203) observe behavior in the live application: how PHP handles a session ID with an invalid character, and how Node.js handles a crafted Brotli payload. Four of the six checks are non-intrusive and can be safely used in production. 

A safe way to verify: The two intrusive checks (QIDs 533068 and 533085) stress the application and can crash an unpatched one. Run them in a QA environment or on a patched production system, through the Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options profile, so verification is a deliberate step with approvals and a maintenance window. 

A ready starting point for the next one: TotalAppSec includes two system-generated option profiles for scanning trending CVEs such as PHP2Shell and Node2Shell. To run a PHP2Shell and Node2Shell web application scan, choose a profile, select your apps by name or tag, and launch. The product tour below walks you through each step. Your scheduled scans may already include the four non-intrusive QIDs, because they are part of the Core, OWASP Top 10 and Everything option profiles and of AI-powered scans. 

Each finding attaches to a named application or API, so its owner can act on it. After the fix and restart, rescan the same applications. If a QID still reports, the patched runtime isn’t the one serving those requests. 

TotalAppSec shows what is exposed at the application and API layer. The runtime underneath lives on hosts, in images and in cloud workloads, where Qualys VMDR, TotalCloud and Container Security find vulnerable PHP and Node.js components. The Qualys Threat Research Unit covers that side in the PHP2Shell and Node.js blogs. 

See It in Action with This Interactive Product Tour 
The Next Runtime Flaw Is Already On Its Way 

PHP2Shell and Node2Shell showed how quickly a flaw in the layer under your applications can become an application risk. The pattern will repeat. The next critical runtime flaw may also sit outside your own code, and attackers will again move faster than most patch cycles. 

The teams that cope best aren’t the ones scrambling hardest in the first week. They already know which web apps and APIs they have, can see which are exposed, and can confirm a fix actually worked. Patched is a claim about a server. Proof is a finding about an application. Qualys TotalAppSec gives you that application-level view, with ready-made trending vulnerability profiles to start from. 

Know Your PHP2Shell Exposure and Mitigate It with Qualys 

Our free service finds PHP2Shell across your internet-facing assets, proves which servers attackers can exploit, and gives you a patch or mitigation path for each one, including versions PHP will never fix.

Get Our Free Services
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) Which option profiles include the PHP2Shell and Node2Shell QIDs? 

The four non-intrusive QIDs (520310, 533086, 520404 and 533203) are in the Trending Vulnerability Options profile, and also in the Core, OWASP Top 10 and Everything option profiles. The two intrusive QIDs (533068 and 533085) are only in Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options. 

Does an AI-powered scan test for the new QIDs? 

Yes, for the four non-intrusive QIDs. The two intrusive QIDs are not part of AI-powered scans, so run them separately with the Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options profile. 

When can a scan miss PHP2Shell or Node2Shell? 

Version-based checks (QIDs 520310 and 520404) can miss an app when a web server or proxy strips response headers and hides the PHP version. The confirmed checks (QIDs 533086 and 533203) test how the application responds instead of reading version headers. 

How do I confirm a fix worked? 

Upgrade the runtime, restart the affected services, then rescan the same applications with Trending Vulnerability Intrusive Options on patched systems or outside production, with approvals and a maintenance window. If a QID is still reported, the fix is incomplete, so check that the patched runtime is serving requests.

items.title: FBI agent stole $2.47m in crypto from criminal wallets
items.summary: .kadence-column487659_4668c2-bd > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column487659_4668c2-bd > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column487659_4668c2-bd > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column487659_4668c2-bd > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column487659_4668c2-bd > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column487659_4668c2-bd > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column487659_4668c2-bd{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column487659_4668c2-bd > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column487659_4668c2-bd > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article A former FBI supervisor stole from cryptocurrency wallets involved in 35 FBI investigations He planned to use the proceeds to finance a new life in Portugal He turned himself in after confessing to a former colleague Law enforcement officers are trusted to handle sensitive evidence properly. A 37-year-old former FBI supervisor used that access to steal millions in cryptocurrency. Patrick Steven Yaroch pleaded guilty on November 5 to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million from cryptocurrency wallets linked to FBI investigations. He stole the money from wallets held by people the FBI was investigating, which included adversarial nation-state actors. Starting no later than December 2024, he made around 100 transfers using credentials tied to 35 separate investigations. The FBI’s search affidavit says that Yaroch accessed FBI systems containing wallet seed phrases and memorized them. A seed phrase is a series of words, commonly 12 or 24, used to restore access to a cryptocurrency wallet. Anyone with the seed phrase can potentially control the funds. He then used the memorized phrases to transfer funds to a personal wallet on his own device. He subsequently swapped assets into different currencies and made further transactions to try and hide their origins. According to the Department of Justice (DOJ), his actions compromised multiple investigations. The affidavit also revealed that Yaroch had asked ChatGPT how to invest a million dollars, along with advice on where to live in Europe. It suggested Portugal, and he began the process of setting up a life there. Caught by a case of cold feet According to the affidavit, he approached a former DOJ colleague to confess because his actions were “eating him up inside.” The employee urged him to self-report, which he did. The FBI placed him on leave and then terminated his employment two days later. They showed up at his home with a warrant and seized assets, including his phone, which had access to a Kraken cryptocurrency account. They also seized a piece of paper containing the seed phrases for his own account. More law enforcement corruption Yaroch’s justification for his initial actions was frustration that the FBI wasn’t acting quickly enough against the wallets’ criminal owners. So he decided to “take matters into his own hands,” according to the affidavit.   • He planned to use the proceeds to finance a new life in Portugal
  • He turned himself in after confessing to a former colleague

Law enforcement officers are trusted to handle sensitive evidence properly. A 37-year-old former FBI supervisor used that access to steal millions in cryptocurrency.

Patrick Steven Yaroch pleaded guilty on November 5 to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million from cryptocurrency wallets linked to FBI investigations.

He stole the money from wallets held by people the FBI was investigating, which included adversarial nation-state actors. Starting no later than December 2024, he made around 100 transfers using credentials tied to 35 separate investigations.

The FBI’s search affidavit says that Yaroch accessed FBI systems containing wallet seed phrases and memorized them. A seed phrase is a series of words, commonly 12 or 24, used to restore access to a cryptocurrency wallet. Anyone with the seed phrase can potentially control the funds.

He then used the memorized phrases to transfer funds to a personal wallet on his own device. He subsequently swapped assets into different currencies and made further transactions to try and hide their origins.

According to the Department of Justice (DOJ), his actions compromised multiple investigations.

The affidavit also revealed that Yaroch had asked ChatGPT how to invest a million dollars, along with advice on where to live in Europe. It suggested Portugal, and he began the process of setting up a life there.

According to the affidavit, he approached a former DOJ colleague to confess because his actions were “eating him up inside.” The employee urged him to self-report, which he did.

The FBI placed him on leave and then terminated his employment two days later. They showed up at his home with a warrant and seized assets, including his phone, which had access to a Kraken cryptocurrency account. They also seized a piece of paper containing the seed phrases for his own account.

More law enforcement corruption

Yaroch’s justification for his initial actions was frustration that the FBI wasn’t acting quickly enough against the wallets’ criminal owners. So he decided to “take matters into his own hands,” according to the affidavit.

But according to the DOJ, he also used some of the proceeds to cover personal debts, including credit cards, car payments, and other loans.

Bridges also pleaded guilty to money laundering and obstruction of justice after stealing bitcoin during the investigation of Silk Road, a dark web marketplace used to sell illegal drugs and other contraband. items.title: Can Agentic AI Investigate a Phishing Campaign? Evidence Walkthrough
items.summary: Yes, with a human signing off. An agentic AI can run most of a phishing investigation on its own. It can pull domain registration records, open the lure safely, pivot to related infrastructure, extract indicators and write up a verdict with the evidence attached. What it shouldn't do yet is act on that verdict unchecked, because attackers are already hiding instructions inside phishing emails meant for the AI doing the reading. The evidence for both halves of that answer is now public. Microsoft's randomized trial of 167 security analysts found that its phishing triage agent made them faster and more accurate. Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that one phishing email can carry a lure for the human and a hidden prompt for the AI in the same message. This post walks through what an agentic investigation of a real phishing campaign looks like, evidence item by evidence item, using the lookalike Microsoft Teams domains that researcher Steven Lim exposed in October. Then it covers where agents break, and what to ask before you trust one. What is an agentic AI security investigation? An agentic AI security investigation is one where an AI agent plans and runs the investigation itself. It decides which data sources to query, calls the tools, reads what comes back, chooses the next step and stops when it can support a verdict with evidence a human can check. The phrase "agentic AI security" also gets used for protecting AI agents from attack. This post is about the other direction: agents doing the investigating. The difference from older automation is who picks the next step. A SOAR playbook runs the same steps every time. A chat assistant answers the question an analyst types. An agent sets its own path based on what it finds, which is exactly what makes it useful and exactly what makes it attackable. SOAR playbook AI chat assistant AI investigation agent Who picks the next step The playbook author, in advance The analyst, one prompt at a time The agent, based on each result What it produces Enrichment fields and tickets Answers and summaries A verdict with an evidence trail Typical failure Breaks on anything off-script Only as good as the questions asked Can be steered by content it reads What the evidence says so far The best public data comes from Microsoft. In November 2025, Microsoft economist James Bono published a randomized controlled trial of the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent. Microsoft recruited 167 professional security analysts and split them into groups that triaged a 25-email queue of real, privacy-vetted user-reported emails, 20% of them malicious, with or without the agent. Analysts working with the agent found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute and were up to 77% more accurate, measured by F1 score. They also spent 53% more time on the malicious emails. The paper found no sign they simply rubber-stamped the agent's calls. Read the fine print before quoting those numbers in a budget meeting. Microsoft studied its own product. On the test corpus, the agent's precision and recall were both 100%, which no production deployment should expect, and the paper's own scenario with a less accurate agent and more malicious mail cut the accuracy gain to 48%. The trial also measured triage: one reported email, one verdict. Investigating a campaign means connecting dozens of artifacts across days, and no comparable trial covers that yet. The skeptical data point comes from Gartner. In June 2025, Gartner predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 over costs, unclear value or weak risk controls. It estimated that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI offer real agentic capabilities, calling the rest "agent washing." Put together: agents have measurable value on narrow, high-volume phishing work, and plenty of products wearing the label won't deliver it. The way to tell them apart is to watch one work a real case. Evidence walkthrough: investigating the fake Teams portals In October 2026, Microsoft Security MVP Steven Lim posted a series of lookalike Microsoft Teams domains on LinkedIn, with screenshots. They make a good test case because the attack never needed a phishing email, so an inbox-only investigation would have missed most of it. Below is the evidence chain an investigation agent should build from that same starting point, one step at a time. It reconstructs the work from the artifacts Lim made public; it is not output from a specific product run. Each step names what the agent does, what it collects and where a human should check. Step 1: Enrich the seed domain The seed is teams-online[.]com. The agent pulls registration data and reputation in parallel. Lim's screenshot gives the answers: registered Oct. 4, 2026, through a privacy service attached to the registrar Global Domain Group, and no active verdict in Microsoft Defender threat intelligence. A lazy agent stops here and calls the domain clean. A good one treats "no verdict" on a four-day-old domain as missing data, not a pass, and weighs what it does know: brand name in the domain, days old, owner hidden. Human check: none yet. This is enrichment, and it's cheap to be wrong here. Step 2: Render the page safely and compare it to the real thing The agent opens the URL in an isolated browser and captures a screenshot, the page source and the assets it loads. The page is a near-copy of the Teams pre-join screen: camera preview, audio options, a "Meeting with the Design team" heading, Sign in and Need help links. The evidence that matters is the comparison. The agent should record which brand assets appear, how closely the layout matches the real join page and whether the page asks for anything (a name, credentials, a download). Human check: confirm the brand match. Visual similarity scoring can flag a legitimate partner page that embeds a Teams meeting. Step 3: Pivot to sibling infrastructure One domain is an incident. Several are a campaign. The agent searches for domains that share traits with the seed: the "teams-" plus generic-word naming pattern, the registrar, hosting, TLS certificates and page templates. Lim's later posts surface two siblings. teams-livemeeting[.]com shared the registrar Global Domain Group, was about 15 days old and was flagged by 3 of 92 vendors in a domain scan. teams-cloud[.]live copied the same Teams join page and was five days old. This is where agents most often overreach. A registrar serves many unrelated customers, so a shared registrar alone proves little. A careful agent links siblings on stronger evidence, such as shared IP addresses, certificate details, identical page code or tracking IDs, and labels each link with its confidence. Lim describes the domains as registered by the same organization; the agent should attribute that claim to him until its own evidence supports it. Human check: review every link the agent marks as "same actor" before anyone writes that in a report. Step 4: Trace how victims reach the pages An email-centered workflow looks for the message that delivered the link. Here there may be no message. Lim reported that teams-livemeeting[.]com surfaced through sponsored search ads and an AI-generated answer, and his screenshot shows a search engine's AI overview citing it beside Microsoft's own links. A later post shows teams-cloud[.]live ranking second in ordinary results for "teams cloud live." The agent should capture these delivery paths as evidence too: the search queries, the ad or result position and the date seen. For practitioners, this maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1583.001 (acquiring domains) and T1608.006 (SEO poisoning). Human check: none for collection. The findings feed the response plan. Step 5: Follow the payload path without detonating blindly On teams-cloud[.]live, joining the meeting led to a fake "You need to update Microsoft Teams" prompt. The Update Teams button downloaded a file named realtek-demo.txt. The agent records the filename, hash and file type, and notes that a text file can't execute on its own. The honest verdict is "staged lure, payload not yet weaponized or swapped per visitor," not "malware delivery." Overstating this step is how investigation reports lose credibility. Human check: decide whether to detonate further, for example by revisiting from a different region or browser profile, since some kits serve payloads selectively. Step 6: Write the verdict and the response plan The output should be a verdict a person can audit in five minutes: three lookalike Teams domains, cloned join pages, delivery through search and ads, a staged fake update, and a confidence level for each claim. The response plan follows from the evidence: block the domains in DNS and web filtering, which is what Lim advised; search proxy and DNS logs for any visits from your users; file takedown requests with the registrar and host; and add the naming pattern to watch lists. Human check: approve every action that touches production or goes outside the company. Blocks are reversible. A takedown request filed under your company's name is not. The evidence ledger This is what the finished case file should contain, and what you should expect any agent to show you. That is the core weakness, and attackers have already found it. Barracuda reported on Oct. 7, that phishing emails in one campaign carried a password-protected attachment for the human and hidden instructions for the AI assistant that summarizes the inbox. Sublime Security documented phishing emails stuffed with invisible text copied from real Adidas newsletters and romance novels, meant to push AI filters toward a benign verdict. StrongestLayer found a malicious file carrying an "LLM_IGNORE_START" comment aimed at AI scanners. Sublime's researchers put the hidden-text technique at under 1% of phishing traffic, so this is early. It is also exactly the input an investigation agent consumes. Three other failure modes show up in practice: Overconfident links. Step 3 is where agents turn a shared registrar into "the same threat actor." A claim without an evidence item behind it should never reach a report. Missing business context. An agent doesn't know that your marketing team runs a microsite on a hyphenated domain, or which vendor portals your staff use. Too much permission. An agent that can file takedowns or change firewall rules on its own turns one poisoned page into an outage or a legal letter. The defenses are design choices you can ask about. Treat everything the agent fetches as data, never as instructions. Separate the permission to read from the permission to act. Require every claim in a verdict to point to an evidence item. Log every tool call so the investigation can be replayed. Keep a human approval step on anything that leaves the building. Seven questions to ask before you trust an investigation agent Gartner's agent-washing estimate means most demos will look impressive. These questions separate an agent that investigates from a chatbot with a playbook behind it. Show me the evidence ledger for a real case. Every claim in the verdict should link to an artifact: a record, a screenshot, a log line. What does it do with a domain that has no reputation yet? If the answer is "marks it clean," it would have passed teams-online[.]com. Can it investigate beyond the inbox? Lookalike domain registrations, search results and ads are delivery channels now. An email-only agent sees part of the campaign. How does it separate content from instructions? Ask what happens when a phishing page or email contains hidden text addressed to the AI. What can it do without human approval? Get the list in writing. Read-only enrichment can be automatic. Blocks, takedowns and user notifications need a person. Can we replay an investigation? You need every query and tool call logged, so an analyst or auditor can retrace the path. What is its accuracy on our data? Vendor benchmarks are best cases; in Microsoft's trial, the agent was 100% accurate on the test corpus. Run a pilot on your own reported phishing and measure false positives and misses yourself. Frequently asked questions Can AI agents investigate phishing on their own? AI agents can gather and correlate most of the evidence in a phishing investigation on their own, including domain records, page captures, related infrastructure and indicators. They should not take outward-facing actions such as takedowns or blocks without human approval, because attackers can plant instructions in the content agents read. How accurate are AI phishing triage agents? In Microsoft's randomized trial with 167 analysts, people working with the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent were up to 77% more accurate and found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute. The agent was 100% accurate on that test corpus, so expect lower numbers in production and measure on your own data. Is agentic AI different from SOAR for phishing response? Yes. A SOAR playbook runs fixed steps written in advance. An AI agent chooses its next step based on what it finds, so it can follow a lead like a sibling domain that no playbook anticipated. That flexibility is also why agents need evidence logging and approval controls. What is the biggest risk of AI agents in security investigations? Prompt injection. An investigation agent reads attacker-controlled emails and web pages, and researchers at Barracuda, Sublime Security and StrongestLayer have documented phishing content with hidden text aimed at AI systems. The fix is design: treat fetched content as data, limit what the agent can do without approval and log every step. Will AI investigation agents replace SOC analysts? The evidence points to a shift in analyst work rather than replacement. In Microsoft's trial, analysts with the agent spent 53% more time on the malicious emails, because the agent handled sorting and first-pass reasoning. Judgment calls on attribution, business context and response still sat with people. Watch an agent work a real case The fake Teams portals show where investigation work has moved. The evidence sat in domain registrations, cloned pages, search results and an AI answer. An agent that only reads the inbox would have seen a fraction of it, and an agent that can't show its evidence shouldn't be trusted with the rest. Blaze AI is Cyble's agentic engine, and it runs across the company's threat intelligence and digital risk protection products, where this kind of outside-in evidence lives. Cyble describes Blaze as correlating threat intelligence and digital risk signals, extracting indicators, and producing decisions that are explainable and auditable. The useful test is the one in this post: give it a seed, watch it build the evidence ledger and see where it asks a human to decide. Get a Blaze AI walkthrough and bring a phishing case of your own.
