Analysts and researchers are advised to confirm once again from original sources.

Can AI agents investigate phishing on their own?

AI agents can gather and correlate most of the evidence in a phishing investigation on their own, including domain records, page captures, related infrastructure and indicators. They should not take outward-facing actions such as takedowns or blocks without human approval, because attackers can plant instructions in the content agents read.

How accurate are AI phishing triage agents?

In Microsoft's randomized trial with 167 analysts, people working with the Security Copilot Phishing Triage Agent were up to 77% more accurate and found up to 6.5 times as many true positives per minute. The agent was 100% accurate on that test corpus, so expect lower numbers in production and measure on your own data.

Is agentic AI different from SOAR for phishing response?

Yes. A SOAR playbook runs fixed steps written in advance. An AI agent chooses its next step based on what it finds, so it can follow a lead like a sibling domain that no playbook anticipated. That flexibility is also why agents need evidence logging and approval controls.

What is the biggest risk of AI agents in security investigations?

Prompt injection. An investigation agent reads attacker-controlled emails and web pages, and researchers at Barracuda, Sublime Security and StrongestLayer have documented phishing content with hidden text aimed at AI systems. The fix is design: treat fetched content as data, limit what the agent can do without approval and log every step.

Will AI investigation agents replace SOC analysts?

The evidence points to a shift in analyst work rather than replacement. In Microsoft's trial, analysts with the agent spent 53% more time on the malicious emails, because the agent handled sorting and first-pass reasoning. Judgment calls on attribution, business context and response still sat with people.

Watch an agent work a real case

The fake Teams portals show where investigation work has moved. The evidence sat in domain registrations, cloned pages, search results and an AI answer. An agent that only reads the inbox would have seen a fraction of it, and an agent that can't show its evidence shouldn't be trusted with the rest.

Blaze AI is Cyble's agentic engine, and it runs across the company's threat intelligence and digital risk protection products, where this kind of outside-in evidence lives. Cyble describes Blaze as correlating threat intelligence and digital risk signals, extracting indicators, and producing decisions that are explainable and auditable. The useful test is the one in this post: give it a seed, watch it build the evidence ledger and see where it asks a human to decide.

Get a Blaze AI walkthrough and bring a phishing case of your own.

  • Gartner, Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027

  • SC Media, Malicious email with prompt injection targets AI-based scanners

items.title: Cofense Advances AI-Driven Phishing Defense with Adaptive Classification and Automation
items.summary: Enhanced AI Classification Engine in Cofense Triage learns from analyst decisions and enables automated processing of high-confidence email classificati ons LEESBURG, Va., November 12, 2026 – Cofense, the leader in AI-driven post-perimeter phishing defense, today announced enhancements to its Phishing Defense Platform with an updated AI Classification Engine (AICE) within its Phishing Remediation solution. AICE uses customer-trained AI to classify reported emails based on an organization's unique categories and enables automated processing of high-confidence decisions. This helps security teams reduce manual triage, accelerate phishing response, and free analysts to focus on complex threats that require human expertise. Unlike static AI models, Cofense’s enhanced AI combines the power of its globally trained phishing detection models with AI trained on an organization’s own analyst decisions and threat environment. Together, these capabilities enable faster, more accurate threat classification and unlock greater automation of phishing response, reducing manual effort while allowing security teams to focus on the threats that matter most. items.title: Apache Patches Critical HTTP/2 Flaw Allowing Remote Code Execution on Web Servers
items.summary: Apache has fixed a critical bug in its HTTP/2 module that could let a remote attacker run code on a web server. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-119618 and affects mod_http2. The fix came on November 11, 2026, in Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71. The bug sits in a function called assign_headers(). Apache says it is a concurrency problem, where shared resources are used without proper locking. Put simply, two parts of the code can touch the same piece of memory at the same time. That can damage the heap, the memory area a program uses while it runs, and this can lead to remote code execution. Apache’s own impact scale reserves the “Critical” label for bugs that a remote attacker could use to run code on a server. These are the kind of bugs that could spread on their own, like a worm. The CVE entry is still marked as reserved, so there is no public CVSS score or detailed technical write-up yet. Admins should not wait for those details before patching. Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 are affected. People who run the standalone mod_h2 from GitHub should check versions 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. Servers that serve HTTP/2 traffic are the main concern, since the flaw lives in that module. Anthropic’s OSS Scanner found the flaw and reported it to the Apache security team on October 26, 2026. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it on their own on November 3. Apache Patches Critical HTTP/2 Flaw Apache released the fix on November 11, about two weeks after the first report. Two teams finding the same bug within days shows how much attention researchers are giving HTTP/2 code. The same release closes two more holes. CVE-2026-106023 is rated “important” and sits in mod_md. A NULL pointer error there can crash a child process while it handles a request, and it affects versions 2.4.30 through 2.4.70. CVE-2026-109163 is a “low” rated one-byte stack overflow in mod_vhost_alias. It affects only versions 2.4.69 and 2.4.70. This is part of a long run of Apache fixes this year. Version 2.4.69 in October fixed 20 CVEs, and 2.4.68 in June fixed 13. Cyber Security News covered the October update in its report on multiple Apache HTTP Server flaws that could enable code execution. HTTP/2 has been a weak spot too. In June, the “HTTP/2 Bomb” denial-of-service exploit hit the default HTTP/2 setups of several popular web servers, including Apache. Many admins who patched in October now have to patch again, only weeks later. That is tiring, but this bug is serious enough to justify it. The best step is to upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 as soon as you can. Start with public-facing servers that have HTTP/2 turned on. Many Linux distributions ship security fixes without changing the version number, so check your vendor’s advisory and package changelog before assuming a server is still exposed. Apache has not listed a workaround for this flaw. If you cannot upgrade right away, one option is to limit the server to HTTP/1.1 until the update is done. Test that change first, because it can affect performance and clients. Also watch your logs for unusual crashes or worker-process restarts, since these can suggest someone is probing the server. The full list of fixed bugs is on Apache’s security vulnerabilities page. The project explains its severity labels on the impact levels page. items.title: Hackers Hijack ConnectWise ScreenConnect to Deploy SCKit Malware Across 288 Devices at 48 Organizations
items.summary: Attackers have taken over cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels and used them to push a custom toolkit called SCKit to at least 288 managed devices across 48 organizations. Security firm Huntress first saw the activity on November 11, 2026, and says all 288 hosts were hit within about 90 minutes. Huntress reports that about one third of them were hit in the first 10 minutes. The attacker used the Run command feature in the ScreenConnect panel to send commands to many endpoints at once. These commands ran with SYSTEM rights, which is the highest level on Windows. The command first checked for an existing ScreenConnect client. It then downloaded a rogue installer to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi and installed it silently. Huntress says it is working with ConnectWise on the case. Reports say the latest ScreenConnect versions, 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, are affected. ConnectWise says it has found no sign that its own systems were broken into and no flaw in ScreenConnect itself. ConnectWise ScreenConnect Hijacked In a public advisory posted on November 11, ConnectWise named five outside extensions that may be tied to the activity. These are Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link. The company turned them off in about 400 partner environments as a safety step. ConnectWise says these extensions offer an API that can run remote commands, and a passphrase set by the partner protects that API. Having an extension installed does not prove a break-in. The company has not yet found the first point of entry or the full scope. Partners who run servers on their own premises must turn the extensions off themselves, because ConnectWise cannot do it for them. SCKit is a package of 16 files, including PowerShell scripts, batch files, and settings data. The infected machine sends its Windows ID to the attacker’s server. The server replies with the key needed to unlock a payload made for that one machine. This makes file hashes a weak way to spot the threat. Next, the scripts install a second rogue ScreenConnect client and add exclusions to Microsoft Defender. They also create a tool called RelayTrap in C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap . A scheduled task named TrapWatch stops the real ScreenConnect client and puts the attacker’s copy in its place. The machine still looks normal to the admin. Huntress also noted that the C# code for RelayTrap looks like it was written with an AI model. The toolkit has a second goal. Huntress found code built to wait until a technician connects to an infected device. It then pulls a dropper onto the technician’s workstation and steals the .aspxauth session cookie. With that cookie, the code tries to reach every other session the technician can open, and it uploads a payload to the panel’s Shared Toolbox. Huntress has not seen this spread work. The console takeover failed in every host log it has checked so far. Still, the design shows why defenders should be careful. This is not the first time criminals have turned ScreenConnect against its users. In September, Cyber Security News covered worm-like rogue ScreenConnect clients that passed staged scripts between Windows machines. Around the same time, CISA added CVE-2026-84869 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. That flaw allows file transfers during a live session without the host’s approval. Huntress says ConnectWise later fixed it, and it scored 9.9 on the CVSS scale. Huntress and ConnectWise give the same core advice. Do not connect to a suspect machine through ScreenConnect, because that session can carry the malware to your own workstation. Use EDR live response, WinRM, or another tool outside ScreenConnect. Teams should also: Isolate affected hosts until cleanup is finished. Huntress saw some machines reinfect after isolation was lifted. Remove the rogue client, the TrapWatch task, the RelayTrap folder, and the RelayTrapLiteAlert Run key. Check Run Command and Toolbox history for jobs nobody started. Revoke active web sessions and rotate credentials from a clean device. Indicators include the domains newnewnew.gotdns[.]org , soxnewwork.homedns[.]org , cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com , and ns.mo7sen[.]dev . They also include the IP address 185.99.255[.]28 and the participant name Addmin . ConnectWise says the investigation is still open and it will update its advisory as facts are confirmed. items.title: Node.js Fixes 16 Security Flaws That Could Expose TLS Private Keys and Crash Servers Remotely
items.summary: The Node.js project has released fixes for 16 security flaws across its 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines. Seven are rated high, six medium, and three low. The official advisory says the patched builds are v22.23.5 , v24.22.3 and v26.13.1 . The update also refreshes three bundled parts: llhttp, undici, and sqlite. Memory Leak Could Expose TLS Private Keys The high-severity flaw is CVE-2026-123864. It affects the HTTPS code in all three lines. A client with no login can read memory that belongs to other connections. That memory can hold TLS private keys and other users’ requests. The cause is a re-entry problem. A zero-length TLS write can make Node.js decrypt the next record while the HTTP parser is still reading a body. This causes a use-after-free and an out-of-bounds read, so the server copies old heap memory into the request body. A server is at risk only if a handler calls res.flushHeaders() early and later ends with a non-empty chunk. A route that echoes or stores request bodies lets the attacker read the leak. Plain node:http is not affected, according to the Node.js security notes . HTTP/2 code accounts for most of the list. CVE-2026-123863 lets any client abort a default HTTP/2 server. It is a variant of CVE-2024-27983 that the older fix missed. CVE-2026-123874 and CVE-2026-123875 hit servers that send files with respondWithFile() . One corrupts memory. The other crashes the server when a download is canceled, and a handful of canceled requests is enough. CVE-2026-123866 can send freed response memory to a peer, which may include other users’ response data. CVE-2026-123865 leaks memory and file descriptors forever once a session fails during shutdown. It repairs a gap left by CVE-2026-48937, which we covered in our June Node.js patch report . Two medium flaws also matter. CVE-2026-123868 lets a client send tiny one-byte frames and make the server keep about 114 bytes for every 10 bytes sent. One stream can then hold hundreds of megabytes. CVE-2026-123828 is a one-byte heap overflow in session.altsvc() that aborts the process when an app passes a long :authority value to it. # CVE Severity Affected Lines Issue 1 CVE-2026-123863 High 24.x, 26.x HTTP/2 session teardown assertion lets a remote client abort the server 2 CVE-2026-123864 High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x HTTPS zero-length TLS write re-enters llhttp and leaks heap memory, including TLS private keys 3 CVE-2026-123865 High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x HTTP/2 sessions never clean up after a protocol error during shutdown, leaking memory and file descriptors 4 CVE-2026-123866 High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x HTTP/2 stream teardown use-after-free sends freed response memory to the peer 5 CVE-2026-126051 High 24.x, 26.x Deferred TLS handshake callbacks cause a remote uncaught exception that kills the server 6 CVE-2026-123872 High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x TLS 1.2 renegotiation lets a client change servername and bypass client certificate checks 7 CVE-2026-123874 High 24.x, 26.x HTTP/2 use-after-free in respondWithFile() streams reset during a pending write 8 CVE-2026-123828 Medium 24.x, 26.x One-byte heap overflow in session.altsvc() with a long origin 9 CVE-2026-123867 Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x CA-only SNI client-CA override falls back to the default CA, bypassing per-host mTLS 10 CVE-2026-123868 Medium 24.x, 26.x HTTP/2 inbound data on an undrained stream escapes maxSessionMemory , allowing memory exhaustion 11 CVE-2026-123871 Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x Proxy credentials exposed in ERR_PROXY_INVALID_CONFIG error messages 12 CVE-2026-123877 Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x https.Agent reuses a TLS session across different CA policies, bypassing certificate validation 13 CVE-2026-123875 Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x Cancelling a respondWithFile() download causes a NULL dereference and crashes the server 14 CVE-2026-123829 Low 22.x, 24.x, 26.x Recursive fs.watch leaks names of files the Permission Model denies (macOS and Windows) 15 CVE-2026-123862 Low 22.x, 24.x, 26.x A pending zlib params() plus destroy() throws an uncatchable assertion and ends the process 16 CVE-2026-106071 Low 22.x, 24.x, 26.x Permission Model wildcard lookup over-grants file system access Login and Certificate Checks Failure Several bugs weaken trust checks. CVE-2026-123872 lets a client switch the server name during TLS 1.2 renegotiation. It can carry a normal login to a host that needs stricter client certificates. CVE-2026-123867 is a related per-host mutual TLS bypass. A host configured with only a CA falls back to the default CA, so the wrong client can get in. CVE-2026-123877 affects https.Agent . A cached TLS session from a broad trust policy can be reused by a request with a stricter policy. The second request then reports authorized === true when it should not. CVE-2026-126051 lets a remote client crash TLS servers that use hooks such as SNICallback or addContext() . CVE-2026-123871 prints proxy credentials inside ERR_PROXY_INVALID_CONFIG errors. That puts secrets into logs and crash reports. It repeats the lesson from CVE-2026-48615. The three low flaws touch the Permission Model and zlib. CVE-2026-123829 leaks file names on macOS and Windows. CVE-2026-106071 lets a wildcard grant match more paths than intended. CVE-2026-123862 can crash an app that calls deflate.params() while streaming, though that use is rare. items.summary_html:
The Node.js project has released fixes for 16 security flaws across its 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines. Seven are rated high, six medium, and three low. The official advisory says the patched builds are v22.23.5, v24.22.3 and v26.13.1. The update also refreshes three bundled parts: llhttp, undici, and sqlite.

Memory Leak Could Expose TLS Private Keys

The high-severity flaw is CVE-2026-123864. It affects the HTTPS code in all three lines. A client with no login can read memory that belongs to other connections. That memory can hold TLS private keys and other users’ requests.

The cause is a re-entry problem. A zero-length TLS write can make Node.js decrypt the next record while the HTTP parser is still reading a body. This causes a use-after-free and an out-of-bounds read, so the server copies old heap memory into the request body.

A server is at risk only if a handler calls res.flushHeaders() early and later ends with a non-empty chunk. A route that echoes or stores request bodies lets the attacker read the leak. Plain node:http is not affected, according to the Node.js security notes.

HTTP/2 code accounts for most of the list. CVE-2026-123863 lets any client abort a default HTTP/2 server. It is a variant of CVE-2024-27983 that the older fix missed. CVE-2026-123874 and CVE-2026-123875 hit servers that send files with respondWithFile(). One corrupts memory. The other crashes the server when a download is canceled, and a handful of canceled requests is enough.

CVE-2026-123866 can send freed response memory to a peer, which may include other users’ response data. CVE-2026-123865 leaks memory and file descriptors forever once a session fails during shutdown. It repairs a gap left by CVE-2026-48937, which we covered in our June Node.js patch report.

Two medium flaws also matter. CVE-2026-123868 lets a client send tiny one-byte frames and make the server keep about 114 bytes for every 10 bytes sent. One stream can then hold hundreds of megabytes. CVE-2026-123828 is a one-byte heap overflow in session.altsvc() that aborts the process when an app passes a long :authority value to it.

#CVESeverityAffected LinesIssue1CVE-2026-123863High24.x, 26.xHTTP/2 session teardown assertion lets a remote client abort the server2CVE-2026-123864High22.x, 24.x, 26.xHTTPS zero-length TLS write re-enters llhttp and leaks heap memory, including TLS private keys3CVE-2026-123865High22.x, 24.x, 26.xHTTP/2 sessions never clean up after a protocol error during shutdown, leaking memory and file descriptors4CVE-2026-123866High22.x, 24.x, 26.xHTTP/2 stream teardown use-after-free sends freed response memory to the peer5CVE-2026-126051High24.x, 26.xDeferred TLS handshake callbacks cause a remote uncaught exception that kills the server6CVE-2026-123872High22.x, 24.x, 26.xTLS 1.2 renegotiation lets a client change servername and bypass client certificate checks7CVE-2026-123874High24.x, 26.xHTTP/2 use-after-free in respondWithFile() streams reset during a pending write8CVE-2026-123828Medium24.x, 26.xOne-byte heap overflow in session.altsvc() with a long origin9CVE-2026-123867Medium22.x, 24.x, 26.xCA-only SNI client-CA override falls back to the default CA, bypassing per-host mTLS10CVE-2026-123868Medium24.x, 26.xHTTP/2 inbound data on an undrained stream escapes maxSessionMemory, allowing memory exhaustion11CVE-2026-123871Medium22.x, 24.x, 26.xProxy credentials exposed in ERR_PROXY_INVALID_CONFIG error messages12CVE-2026-123877Medium22.x, 24.x, 26.xhttps.Agent reuses a TLS session across different CA policies, bypassing certificate validation13CVE-2026-123875Medium22.x, 24.x, 26.xCancelling a respondWithFile() download causes a NULL dereference and crashes the server14CVE-2026-123829Low22.x, 24.x, 26.xRecursive fs.watch leaks names of files the Permission Model denies (macOS and Windows)15CVE-2026-123862Low22.x, 24.x, 26.xA pending zlib params() plus destroy() throws an uncatchable assertion and ends the process16CVE-2026-106071Low22.x, 24.x, 26.xPermission Model wildcard lookup over-grants file system access Login and Certificate Checks Failure

Several bugs weaken trust checks. CVE-2026-123872 lets a client switch the server name during TLS 1.2 renegotiation. It can carry a normal login to a host that needs stricter client certificates. CVE-2026-123867 is a related per-host mutual TLS bypass. A host configured with only a CA falls back to the default CA, so the wrong client can get in.

CVE-2026-123877 affects https.Agent. A cached TLS session from a broad trust policy can be reused by a request with a stricter policy. The second request then reports authorized === true when it should not.

CVE-2026-126051 lets a remote client crash TLS servers that use hooks such as SNICallback or addContext(). CVE-2026-123871 prints proxy credentials inside ERR_PROXY_INVALID_CONFIG errors. That puts secrets into logs and crash reports. It repeats the lesson from CVE-2026-48615.

The three low flaws touch the Permission Model and zlib. CVE-2026-123829 leaks file names on macOS and Windows. CVE-2026-106071 lets a wildcard grant match more paths than intended. CVE-2026-123862 can crash an app that calls deflate.params() while streaming, though that use is rare.

Researcher Chris Rohlf, working with Claude and Anthropic Research, reported five of the 16 flaws. Other reporters include Pimterry, Trail of Bits, and several independent researchers. Matteo Collina fixed most of them.

This release followed a short warning. Our earlier story on the scheduled patch noted that the notice gave no CVE details. The full list is now public. October’s Node2Shell Brotli bug and July’s 11 fixes show that Node.js ships serious fixes almost every month.

Upgrade to v22.23.5, v24.22.3, or v26.13.1 first. Public HTTP/2 and HTTPS servers should go first. Then rebuild container images so they carry the new runtime. Teams that served traffic from a vulnerable HTTPS handler should consider replacing their TLS keys, since leaked memory leaves no clear trace. End-of-life versions are always affected, so move off them. The Node.js release schedule lists support dates.

items.title: Smashing Security podcast #492: How hackers turned Russian cars into pumpkins
items.summary: You're driving your new Chinese SUV when the dashboard goes dark. Ten minutes later, your phone rings. A stranger says they've got the digital key to your car, and would you like it back? Of course you would. That'll be $550. Meanwhile, three men have been charged over a scheme that used deepfakes of company bosses to steal around $130 million. Hear more about what happened, and the simple human trick that can foil the fakes. All this and more in episode 492 of the "Smashing Security" podcast with cybersecurity expert and keynote speaker Graham Cluley, and special guest Danny Palmer.

items.title: How 1Password for Agents preserves security and privacy
items.summary: People have trusted 1Password with the credentials behind their digital lives for years. How does 1Password extend that trust to AI agent access while ensuring that the customer is always in control of their information and how it’s accessed? As Ethan Mollick , a professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, puts it, “The agentic web is here earlier than people expected.” It seems like every day, AI agents are able to do more to interact with systems and take action for users, but the speed of their development has left traditional security falling behind . To be useful, agents need access to your accounts. For instance, an agent can plan a trip for you, but would need access to your desired airline account or favorite travel booking website to do so. The value of such use-cases is clear, but giving agents access should not require that you let them see or store your credentials. Pasting your password into a prompt means allowing the agent to have access to your credential, potentially beyond the task at hand. What’s needed now more than ever is a secure, seamless way to approve sign-ins for personal agents to access accounts they need to carry out tasks, all without exposing login credentials to the agent. 1Password solves this through 1Password for Agents , which enables users to safely provide access to AI agents like Muse, from Meta, SpaceXSI Grok Bot, and Town. 1Password for Agents makes secure sign-in standard for the personal AI agents people use today. How AI agents sign in without seeing your passwords Personal AI agents can plan trips, manage calendars, organize events, and complete tasks across the websites and services you use every day. But to do that work, agents need access to the accounts you want them to interface with. That creates a dilemma: how can an agent act on your behalf without taking possession of your passwords or compromising your security and privacy? The answer lies in 1Password for Agents’ security model , which is built upon the fundamental 1Password security model that’s trusted by millions to protect how they live and work. Everything 1Password does is guided by principles that put your safety first. One of these principles is that only you should have the keys required to the data you store in 1Password. Here’s how authorization is built to stay true to the principles of those security models so that: 1Password securely stores your credentials Agents can’t see your credentials at sign-in Agents cannot autonomously interact with your vault Connecting your account To connect an agent app, you sign into 1Password. When you connect the accounts, your device then creates keys for the connection and encrypts them with a new integration key. 1Password stores the encrypted keys. Only the agent developer receives the integration key, so 1Password can’t decrypt them. These keys ensure that, as always, all vault data is encrypted at rest. Stopping agent access: At any time, you can go into the agent’s app and disconnect 1Password. This deletes the connection’s keys, every associated approval, and revokes the agent’s access to your account. Approving which login an AI agent can use Once the connection and keys are in place, an agent has to follow a set process to sign in through a browser without handling one of your vault items. The agent reaches a sign-in page and requests a specific login. The 1Password app shows you an approval prompt describing what the agent is asking for and which saved login could help. You approve or deny the request. If you approve, 1Password browser extension fills and submits the specific password or one-time code directly into the destination. The agent is signed in and keeps working without seeing the password or the rest of your vault. 1Password for Agents delivers the approved vault login to the 1Password browser extension, so that the agent knows it received permission to sign in. The login remains protected because the agent can't see the underlying password. Preventing unapproved vault access through the browser extension Protecting the credential is only part of the problem. When an agent controls a browser, could it also try to interact with other credentials in your 1Password vault? 1Password and the agent app each have a role in protecting your logins. 1Password’s guarantees cover the storage, approval, delivery, and filling of credentials. We provide the agent with the credentials you’ve approved and only on matching pages, submit right away, and clear values from the page if submission fails. After a successful fill, what the agent does on the website is governed by the agent’s own safeguards. The agent developer stores the authorization tokens and integration key for your connection, and their agent controls the environment into which items are filled. All 1Password for Agents providers have signed an agreement to uphold shared security principles with 1Password and passed a security review. 1Password’s trusted access layer for personal agents Personal AI agents become more useful when they have more access. They also pose more risk. Using an agent should not require that you let the agent see your bank passwords or any other credentials. This ensures that your plaintext credentials are never kept in the agent’s context or application logs; the agent can’t use or store your passwords or credentials without your oversight. 1Password is extending the security role it has always played for credentials and applying it to personal agents. Your vault remains the source of truth, and you remain the decision-maker. 1Password for Agents gives agents a controlled way to request access and lets them sign in without seeing your credentials or passwords. You can control what AI agents access and when, without letting them take advantage of your personal information. Want to learn more? Explore the 1Password for Agents security documentation to learn more about how connectors and authorization requests work. Read the documentation

People have trusted 1Password with the credentials behind their digital lives for years. How does 1Password extend that trust to AI agent access while ensuring that the customer is always in control of their information and how it’s accessed?

As Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, puts it, “The agentic web is here earlier than people expected.” It seems like every day, AI agents are able to do more to interact with systems and take action for users, but the speed of their development has left traditional security falling behind.

To be useful, agents need access to your accounts. For instance, an agent can plan a trip for you, but would need access to your desired airline account or favorite travel booking website to do so. The value of such use-cases is clear, but giving agents access should not require that you let them see or store your credentials. Pasting your password into a prompt means allowing the agent to have access to your credential, potentially beyond the task at hand.

What’s needed now more than ever is a secure, seamless way to approve sign-ins for personal agents to access accounts they need to carry out tasks, all without exposing login credentials to the agent.

1Password solves this through 1Password for Agents, which enables users to safely provide access to AI agents like Muse, from Meta, SpaceXSI Grok Bot, and Town. 1Password for Agents makes secure sign-in standard for the personal AI agents people use today.

How AI agents sign in without seeing your passwords

Personal AI agents can plan trips, manage calendars, organize events, and complete tasks across the websites and services you use every day. But to do that work, agents need access to the accounts you want them to interface with.

That creates a dilemma: how can an agent act on your behalf without taking possession of your passwords or compromising your security and privacy?

The answer lies in 1Password for Agents’ security model, which is built upon the fundamental 1Password security model that’s trusted by millions to protect how they live and work. Everything 1Password does is guided by principles that put your safety first. One of these principles is that only you should have the keys required to the data you store in 1Password.

Here’s how authorization is built to stay true to the principles of those security models so that:

  • 1Password securely stores your credentials

  • Agents can’t see your credentials at sign-in

  • Agents cannot autonomously interact with your vault

Connecting your account

To connect an agent app, you sign into 1Password. When you connect the accounts, your device then creates keys for the connection and encrypts them with a new integration key. 1Password stores the encrypted keys. Only the agent developer receives the integration key, so 1Password can’t decrypt them.

These keys ensure that, as always, all vault data is encrypted at rest.

Stopping agent access: At any time, you can go into the agent’s app and disconnect 1Password. This deletes the connection’s keys, every associated approval, and revokes the agent’s access to your account.

Approving which login an AI agent can use

Once the connection and keys are in place, an agent has to follow a set process to sign in through a browser without handling one of your vault items.

  • The agent reaches a sign-in page and requests a specific login.

  • The 1Password app shows you an approval prompt describing what the agent is asking for and which saved login could help.

  • You approve or deny the request.

  • If you approve, 1Password browser extension fills and submits the specific password or one-time code directly into the destination.

  • The agent is signed in and keeps working without seeing the password or the rest of your vault.

1Password for Agents delivers the approved vault login to the 1Password browser extension, so that the agent knows it received permission to sign in. The login remains protected because the agent can't see the underlying password.

Preventing unapproved vault access through the browser extension

Protecting the credential is only part of the problem. When an agent controls a browser, could it also try to interact with other credentials in your 1Password vault?

1Password and the agent app each have a role in protecting your logins. 1Password’s guarantees cover the storage, approval, delivery, and filling of credentials. We provide the agent with the credentials you’ve approved and only on matching pages, submit right away, and clear values from the page if submission fails. After a successful fill, what the agent does on the website is governed by the agent’s own safeguards. The agent developer stores the authorization tokens and integration key for your connection, and their agent controls the environment into which items are filled. All 1Password for Agents providers have signed an agreement to uphold shared security principles with 1Password and passed a security review.

1Password’s trusted access layer for personal agents

Personal AI agents become more useful when they have more access. They also pose more risk. Using an agent should not require that you let the agent see your bank passwords or any other credentials. This ensures that your plaintext credentials are never kept in the agent’s context or application logs; the agent can’t use or store your passwords or credentials without your oversight.

1Password is extending the security role it has always played for credentials and applying it to personal agents. Your vault remains the source of truth, and you remain the decision-maker. 1Password for Agents gives agents a controlled way to request access and lets them sign in without seeing your credentials or passwords.

You can control what AI agents access and when, without letting them take advantage of your personal information.

Want to learn more?

Explore the 1Password for Agents security documentation to learn more about how connectors and authorization requests work.
